docs.title: HapSelect
docs.text:
HapSelect is an R package for haploblock-based genomic selection. It processes inpute genomic and phenotypic files, partitions the genome into blocks (haploblocks), estimates regional genetic value using either a localGEBV framework or a true haplotype-effect framework, identifies high-value genomic regions, optimizes parent selection using a genetic algorithm, and performs simulation to compare alternative selection strategies.

The package is designed for breeding programs running genomic selection, where identifying and targeting the genomic regions with the most exploitable diversity can improve the efficiency of parent choice.

docs.title: Workflow at a glance
docs.text:
Stage What it does Key function Data Import (optional) Read VCF files, and impute and phase genotypes with BEAGLE read_vcf_geno() / beagle_phase_geno() Pairwise LD Compute r² between all marker pairs pairwise_ld() / plink_pairwise_ld_geno() Haploblocking Partition genome into haploblocks using LD-based, window-based, or graph-based blocking def_blocks() with ld_strategy(), window_strategy(), or graph_strategy() / block_obj_to_df() Genomic Prediction Compute marker effects and prediction accuracy create_marker_effects_file(), n_fold_cross_validation(), cross_validation() LocalGEBV/Haplotype Effect Estimate per-block GEBV or haplotype effects per individual compute_local_GEBV() / compute_haplotype_effects() Visualisation Explore haploblock structure, localGEBV/haplotype patterns, and more plot_haploblocks(), plot_haploblocks_variance(), plot_ld_decay(), … Parent selection Optimise parent selection using a genetic algorithm local_gebv_parent_selection() / haplotype_parent_selection() Basic Simulation Compare GA and TS parent performance over time and explore how diversity is captured using the genomicSimulation R package. localGEBV_vs_TS_simulation() / Haplotype_vs_TS_simulation()

See the Overview for a full explanation of the method, or jump to Getting Started to run the example workflow.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
1. Download and extract the .zip file here: HapSelect

  2. Ensure RTools 4.5 (Windows) and genomicSimulation are installed and the OPTIONAL PLINK 1.9 bin and BEAGLE .jar files are in the bin folder in your home directory (~/bin, or C:/Users/<username>/bin on Windows) or a folder on the system PATH. Alternatively, point HapSelect at them with set_plink_path() and set_beagle_path() (see Configuration).

  3. Non-Windows machines must have a C++ compiler compatible with the Rcpp R package.

  4. This is usually detected automatically and shipped natively with Linux/Unix and macOS systems.

  5. Either set the working directory in R with: setwd("path/to/unzipped/file/HapSelect/") (if nested inside the extracted folder) or record the full path to the unzipped directory.

Install with base R command:

#setting the working directory
setwd("/path/to/unzipped/file/HapSelect/") #if the extracted main folder remains
install.packages("HapSelect", type = "source", repos = NULL)

Warning

genomicSimulation, RTools 4.5 (for Windows users), PLINK 1.9 (optional), and BEAGLE (optional) dependencies must be installed separately. Alternatively run the helper installation scripts to install all required software. The package is usable without PLINK 1.9 or BEAGLE, but related functions that call PLINK and/or BEAGLE will fail with an error. See Installation for more details.

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text: All notable changes to HapSelect are documented here. This project follows the Keep a Changelog format.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• graphing haploblocking strategy added to def_blocks() for alternative haploblocking strategies
  • window-based haploblocking (physical/genetic distance based on the map or number of SNP) added to def_blocks() for alternative haploblocking strategies
  • strategy argument with method-specific container function call added to def_blocks() to differentiate methodology used for haploblocking
  • HapSelect R package text banner added on load
  • Rudimentary imputation and phasing using a BEAGLE backbone added to simplify workflows: beagle_impute_geno() and beagle_phase_geno() (imputes and phases)
  • VCF read functions added for file importation simplicity (Note: does not currently handle aneuploidy or variable ploidy): read_vcf_geno(), read_vcf_phased()
  • Visualization for haploblock variance on physical/genetic chromosome location added to explore regional variance and block size: plot_haploblocks_variance()
  • Limitations to CPU handlers and machine-readable step reporting added: set_cpu_cores(), cpu_cores(), and the HAPSELECT_MACHINE_LOGGING event stream (see Configuration and Progress Reporting)
  • Custom C++ LD computation added to remove reliance on PLINK backbone: pairwise_ld() with C++ backbone, with new window, min_r2, and min_obs arguments
  • order_geno() added to put a genotype file in the same order as the map
  • Functions to set PLINK executable/binary and BEAGLE .jar file locations added: set_beagle_path() and set_plink_path()
  • Added more file and input checks, more informative error messages
  • Actual wheat example input files added
  • More extensive testthat coverage to ensure future updates produce viable code

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• Fixed bug that produced NA prediction accuracy if any BLUE/adj phenotype/de-regressed BLUP inputs were NA
  • Small reporting or file error bugs fixed (note nothing that would affect any results users see)
  • Some conflicts between example input files and old input files that were not updated are now updated and correct
  • cross_validation() no longer fails when fold is left at its default value

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• Step Reporting and progress reporting updated
  • def_blocks() function syntax changed to support evolving haploblocking strategies
  • detection of PLINK improved
  • updated graphical progress bar calls to reduce RStudio GUI performance impacts
  • order_map() will now coerce chromosomes to numerics and report
  • many issues with files will now report inputs causing issues (e.g., markers missing from the map file)
  • PLINK and BEAGLE are limited to the number of cores allowed by set_cpu_cores()
  • simulation temporary files are now written to R's temporary directory rather than the working directory

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
HapSelect has a small number of session-wide settings: where to find the optional external tools (PLINK and BEAGLE) and how many CPU cores it may use. Every setting lasts for the current R session only. See Making settings permanent to apply them every time R starts.

Function Description set_plink_path(path) Use a specific PLINK 1.9 executable set_beagle_path(path) Use a specific BEAGLE 5.5 .jar file set_cpu_cores(cores) Limit the number of CPU cores HapSelect may use cpu_cores() Report the number of CPU cores HapSelect will use

docs.title: How PLINK and BEAGLE are found
docs.text:
PLINK (for plink_pairwise_ld() and plink_pairwise_ld_geno()) and BEAGLE (for the beagle_*() functions) are optional. When one is needed, HapSelect searches the following locations in order and uses the first match:

  1. The location given to set_plink_path() / set_beagle_path()
  2. The bin folder in your home directory used by the install scripts (~/bin on Linux/macOS, C:/Users/<username>/bin on Windows)
  3. Every folder on the system PATH

Each candidate is checked by actually running it. PLINK must report version 1.9 and BEAGLE must report version 5.5 - anything else is skipped (or, for a location you set yourself, is an error). BEAGLE also needs a Java runtime available on the PATH. See Installation for how to install both tools.

docs.title: set_plink_path()
docs.text:
set_plink_path(path = "C:/Users/<username>/tools/plink.exe")  #the executable
set_plink_path(path = "C:/Users/<username>/tools")            #or the folder containing it

set_plink_path(path = NULL)                                   #clear the setting and search automatically again

docs.title: set_beagle_path()
docs.text:
set_beagle_path(path = "C:/Users/<username>/tools/beagle.27Feb25.75f.jar")  #the .jar file
set_beagle_path(path = "C:/Users/<username>/tools")                         #or the folder containing it

set_beagle_path(path = NULL)                                                #clear the setting and search automatically again
Parameter Default Description path NULL Path to the executable / .jar file, or the folder containing it. NULL clears the setting

Both functions check the tool straight away and stop with an error if it cannot be found or is the wrong version, in which case the previous setting is kept. On success, they invisibly return the full path that will be used. The path is checked again every time the tool is run, in case it has been moved or upgraded since.

Tip

On Windows, the PLINK check also catches a common mix-up: the PuTTY suite ships its own program called plink.exe, which is not PLINK. If set_plink_path() reports "This may not be PLINK, do you have PuTTY installed?", point it at the PLINK 1.9 executable directly.

docs.title: set_cpu_cores()
docs.text:
By default, HapSelect may use every core available to the R session. set_cpu_cores() sets a ceiling on that for the rest of the session, which is useful on shared machines or when running other jobs alongside HapSelect.

set_cpu_cores(cores = 4)     #use at most 4 cores
set_cpu_cores(cores = NULL)  #clear the limit and use every available core
Parameter Default Description cores NULL Maximum number of cores, a number ≥ 1 (fractions are rounded down). NULL clears the limit

The limit is a ceiling, not a target: HapSelect never uses more cores than are actually available, so setting a limit higher than the machine has does nothing.

Tip

"Available" cores come from future::availableCores(), which already respects limits set by job schedulers such as SLURM or PBS (e.g., SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK) and R's mc.cores option. On a cluster you will usually not need set_cpu_cores() at all.

docs.title: cpu_cores()
docs.text:
Returns the number of cores HapSelect will use, after applying the limit.

cpu_cores()
#> [1] 4

docs.title: What the limit applies to
docs.text:
Function Parallel option Notes pairwise_ld() parallelize = TRUE One worker per core, split by chromosome ld_strategy() / graph_strategy() parallel = TRUE Split by chromosome, so never more workers than chromosomes compute_local_GEBV() / compute_haplotype_effects() parallel = TRUE Blocks are split into chunks across workers plink_pairwise_ld() / plink_pairwise_ld_geno() always Passed to PLINK as --threads, unless --threads is given in extra_args beagle_impute() / beagle_impute_geno() / beagle_phase_geno() always Passed to BEAGLE as nthreads=, unless nthreads= is given in extra_args

Warning

Each parallel worker is a separate R process with its own copy of the data it is given. On large datasets, memory rather than the number of cores is often the limiting factor - if R runs out of memory in parallel mode, lower set_cpu_cores() (or, for localGEBV, chunk_size).

docs.title: BEAGLE, PLINK, and parallelisation Options
docs.text:
Every setting above is stored as an R option, so you can apply them every time R starts by adding the options to your .Rprofile file (e.g., with usethis::edit_r_profile()):

options(
  HapSelect.plink_path  = "C:/Users/<username>/tools/plink.exe",
  HapSelect.beagle_path = "C:/Users/<username>/tools/beagle.27Feb25.75f.jar",
  HapSelect.cpu_cores   = 4
)

Options set this way are checked the first time they are used, rather than when they are set.

docs.title: Progress Bar Updates
docs.text:
HapSelect throttles progress bar updates by default to avoid sending too many updates to the RStudio GUI. On large or computationally intensive operations with many small, incremental updates, frequent progress updates can introduce unnecessary overhead and cause the RStudio interface to become sluggish and, at worst, freeze.

You can increase the minimum time between progress bar updates by setting HapSelect.progress_interval. This makes updates less frequent, which can improve responsiveness when running long operations. However, the default value of 0.2 seconds should be sufficient for the vast majority of users:

Option Default Description HapSelect.progress_interval 0.2 Minimum time between progress bar updates, in seconds. Increase this value to reduce update frequency.

For example, to update the progress bar at most every second:

options(
  HapSelect.progress_interval = 1
)

Add this option to your .Rprofile alongside the other settings to make it permanent. A value of 0.2 (200 ms) is the default.

docs.title: Startup Banner
docs.text:
HapSelect prints a banner with the installed version and a link to the matching version of this documentation when it is attached with library(HapSelect). To load it silently (e.g., in scripts):

suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(HapSelect))

Tip

Features and functions differ between versions. Always use the documentation for your installed version - the version selector at the top of this site, or the link in the banner, will take you there. packageVersion("HapSelect") reports the installed version.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: This page walks through the complete HapSelect using localGEBV or haplotypes using the built-in example datasets.

docs.title: Load the Package
docs.text: library(HapSelect)

docs.title: Required Data
docs.text:
HapSelect expects two primary inputs (map file and genotype file). The rest can be computed in the R package or externally as additional inputs:

  • Map file — marker positions with columns for marker ID, chromosome, and position.

    • First column should be named SNP and should be a character vector, not numeric or factorized.
    • Second column should be named Chromosome and should be numeric for proper sorting.
    • Third column should be named Position and should be numeric. It can be a physical position or genetic map position.

  • Genotype matrix (localGEBV) — markers × individuals, coded as allele dosage (0/1/2 for diploid, 0/1/.../n for polyploid) at a biallelic marker.

    • First three columns should be identical to the map file.
    • Columns 4:ncol(genotype_file) should be individuals and their genotype for each marker (rows are markers, columns are individuals).
    • Names of columns 4 onwards should be the individuals' identifiers.
    • Genotypes should be dosage format: i.e., number of copies of the alternative allele (integer counts only for consistency).
    • NA values are allowed and are handled differently at each stage via options in the relevant functions.

  • Phased genotype matrix (haplotypes) — markers × chromosomes coded as the allele (0 for reference, 1 for alternative) at a biallelic marker.

    • First three columns should be identical to the map file.
    • Names of columns 4 onwards should be the individuals' chromosomal identifiers. The nomencalture adopted in HapSelect is individualID_chromosomeNum as the identifier, where the last _ in the string is used to identify the chromosome.
    • Alleles should be dosage format: i.e., 0 for the reference allele and 1 for the alternative allele.
    • NA values are allowed and are handled differently at each stage via options in the relevant functions.

Warning

Computing LD, haploblocks, and haplotype effects are supported for polyploids in localGEBV and haplotype methods, but parent selection algorithms and simulation currently only support diploid! We plan to update the localGEBV method to support polyploidy in the near future and the haplotype method at an indeterminate date.

  • LD file - pairwise LD between each marker within a chromosome.

    • Only required for LD-based blocking (ld_strategy()) and the LD decay plot. Window-based blocking needs no LD, and graph-based blocking computes its own.
    • Can be computed internally using either the in-built C++ function (pairwise_ld()) or the PLINK 1.9 wrapper function (plink_pairwise_ld_geno()).
    • Can be computed externally and read in (see file structure below)
    • Pairs not present (i.e., missing) in the data frame object are allowed and are handled in the haploblocking function call.
    • Columns:
      • Chrom: the chromosome each SNP pair belongs to.
      • Locus1: numerical integer for the first marker in the marker pair. This should correspond to the order of the marker in the ordered map file (see below for more details).
      • Locus2: similar to Locus1, this is the numerical integer of the second marker in the marker pair.
      • Name1: Character name of the first marker in the pair as seen in the genotype, map, and marker effects file.
      • Name2: Similar to Name1, this corresponds to the name of the second marker in the pair as seen in the genotype, map, and marker effects file.
      • LD: The numerical LD value computed. This is typically an \(R^{2}\) value.

  • Marker effects file — estimated SNP effects from a genomic prediction model

    • Can be computed for basic cases in the package (localGEBV genotype dosage matrix only!) with BLUE/dergressed BLUP/singular adjusted phenotype or provided externally.
    • First column: SNP corresponding to the SNP column in the map and genotype file. It should be formatted as a character vector.
    • Second column: Effect the allele substitution (marker) effects corresponding to the SNP in column one. This is the allele subsitution effect when subsituting one reference (0) allele with one alternative (1) allele.

Warning

Ensure that the genotype coding in the genotype matrix is the same that was utilised to estimate marker effects. Marker effects computed within the package will be the same as long as the genotype matrix was not changed post-estimation.

  • Haploblock file - dataframe produced as a standard part of the workflow.
    • May be provided if custom haploblocking is desired. Blocking by LD, by physical/map distance or number of markers, and by a local LD graph are all built in (see Haplotype Blocks).
    • Columns:
      • Block: SNP names within a block as identified in the map, genotype, and marker effects files. They should be separated by a ";" (no whitespaces as this will break downstream computations!). It must be a character!
      • Block_ID: Unique block identifier. We utilise the format "chromosome:block_nested_within_chromosome". As an example, "3:132" corresponds to the 132nd block on chromosome 3. It must be a character!
      • Num_SNP: The number of SNP in the block (number of markers in Block, must be numeric).
      • First_SNP: The first marker (based on physical/map position) in the block (must be a character).
      • Last_SNP: The last marker (based on physical/map position) in the block (must be a character).
      • Chrom: Numerical value of the chromosome the block resides on.
      • Start_Pos: The numerical position of First_SNP (usually physical or genetic map position).
      • End_Pos: The numerical position of Last_SNP (usually physical or genetic map position).

Tip

If your genotypes are in a VCF file, read_vcf_geno() and read_vcf_phased() will read them into these formats, and beagle_phase_geno() will impute and phase them. See Data Import, Imputation, and Phasing.

Example datasets are bundled with the package along with function examples to compute other files:

#Two required, primary inputs:
map  <- HapSelect::map
geno        <- HapSelect::geno        #localGEBV
geno_phased <- HapSelect::geno_phased #haplotype method

#Optional inputs that can also be created in the R package workflow:
ld_pairs       <- HapSelect::ld_pairs
marker_effects <- HapSelect::marker_effects
BLUE           <- HapSelect::BLUE #example file to compute marker effects

#Haploblock dataframe can be computed by running the def_blocks() and block_obj_to_df() functions on the example data

docs.title: Step 1 — Order the Map
docs.text:
Markers must be sorted by chromosome and position before LD computation, and the genotype files put in the same order:

map         <- order_map(map = map)
geno        <- order_geno(geno = geno, map = map)
geno_phased <- order_geno(geno = geno_phased, map = map)

docs.title: Step 2 — Compute Pairwise LD
docs.text:
# Internal R implementation with C++ backend
ld_pairs   <- pairwise_ld(
  genotype_matrix = geno,
  parallelize     = FALSE,
  window          = NULL,
  min_r2          = NULL,
  min_obs         = 2L
)

# PLINK-backed implementation (requires PLINK 1.9, see Installation and Configuration)
ld_pairs   <- plink_pairwise_ld_geno(
  geno           = geno,
  ld_window      = 999999,
  ld_window_kb   = 1e6,
  ld_window_r2   = 0
)

docs.title: Step 3 — Define Haplotype Blocks
docs.text:
#LD Blocking
haploblocks <- def_blocks(
  map         = map,
  strategy    = ld_strategy(
    ld        = ld_pairs,
    method    = "flanking",
    tolerance = 3,
    threshold = 0.5,
    start     = "beginning",
    tol_reset = TRUE,
    parallel  = FALSE
  )
)

#### Window-Based Blocking #####

#make a haploblock list object

#using fixed physical distance of cM widths, depending on the map
haploblocks <- def_blocks(
  map         = map,
  strategy    = window_strategy(
    window    = 100000, # 100kb window
    method    = "window_map"
  )
)

#using fixed SNP intervals
haploblocks <- def_blocks(
  map         = map,
  strategy    = window_strategy(
    window    = 50, # every 50 SNP
    method    = "window_snp"
  )
)

#Graph-based blocking (LD calculated internally - geno is required)
haploblocks <- def_blocks(
  map          = map,
  geno         = geno,
  strategy     = graph_strategy(
    theta_core        = 0.80,
    theta_core_by_chr = NULL,
    theta_extend      = 0.20,
    theta_bridge      = 0.20,
    theta_refill      = 0.80,
    ld_min_r2         = 0.20,
    window_ld         = 20,
    window_core       = 20,
    window_extend     = 50,
    min_links         = 1,
    max_gap_snps      = 2,
    max_gap_markers   = 2,
    max_gap_position  = NULL,
    min_block_snps    = 2,
    parallel          = FALSE
  )
)


#turn object into an interpretable
haploblocks <- block_obj_to_df(haploblocks, map)

#Report basic block statistics:
block_summary(block_df = haploblocks)

#Note: Mean_Block_Size does not include singleton blocks (size 0) in the computation. It is the mean size of multi-SNP blocks.

docs.title: Step 4 — Compute localGEBV/haplotype effects
docs.text:
#localGEBV
haploblock_obj <- compute_local_GEBV(
  geno           = geno,
  marker_effects = marker_effects,
  haploblocks_df = haploblocks,
  set_missing_NA = TRUE,            #if TRUE, any missing genotypes in a block will return NA for the localGEBV
  mean_adjust    = TRUE             #centeres the genotype matrix - this should be TRUE in almost every case! Setting to FALSE will lead to biased localGEBV!
)

#haplotypes
haplotype_obj <- compute_haplotype_effects(
  geno           = geno_phased,
  marker_effects = marker_effects,
  haploblocks_df = haploblocks,
  set_missing_NA = TRUE,            #if TRUE, any missing alleles in a block will return NA for the haplotype effect
  mean_adjust    = TRUE             #centeres the allele matrix - this should be TRUE in almost every case! Setting to FALSE will lead to biased haplotype effects!
)

Tip

Check out the full workflow if you need a basic model to compute marker effects (localGEBV genotype matrix only!).

docs.title: Step 5 — Visualise
docs.text:
#Manhattan-style plot of allele subsitution effects
marker_effects_plot(marker_effects = marker_effects$Effect,
                    chr = map$Chromosome, pos = map$Position)

#Manhattan-style plots of localGEBV and haplotype effects
unique_haplo_effects_plot(haplo_obj = haplotype_obj)      #haplotypes
unique_localGEBV_effects_plot(haplo_obj = haploblock_obj) #localGEBV

#Visualization of block sizes and block positions
plot_haploblocks(haploblock_df = haploblock_obj$Haploblocks)

#Visualization of block sizes, positions, and variance (after calculating localGEBV/haplotype effects)
block_variance_manhattan_plot(
  haplo_obj = haploblock_obj
)
plot_haploblocks_variance(haploblock_obj = haploblock_obj)

#Tornado plots demonstrating the spread of localGEBV and haplotype effects with blocks ordered by variance
haplo_block_var_funnel_plot(haplo_obj = haplotype_obj, mean_line = FALSE) #haplotypes
local_gebv_block_var_funnel_plot(haplo_obj = haploblock_obj, mean_line = FALSE)

#Plot to visualize LD decay
plot_ld_decay(map = map, ld = ld_pairs, max_kb = 500) #warning: may be slow for large dataset! Use method = "exp" for faster computation and monotonic decay. For a more flexible and still relatively quick approach, explore, method = "gam_tp".

Tip

All plots return a ggplot object. Positions for localGEBV/haplotype effects, haploblocks, and marker densities are in absolute units to accomodate both physical and genetic maps. All ggplots can be modified to change axis scale, legend name, axis name, etc. See Visualisations for examples.

docs.title: Step 6 — Select Top Blocks and Parents
docs.text:
Tip

Generally, a small subset of blocks explains the vast majority of total variance in localGEBV. While the whole genome can be used for optimisation, results are often completley identical and it is much more computationally efficient to use a subset of blocks. In past examples, 9-13% of blocks have explaind at least 90% of genetic variance.

#There are three methods we have implemented to select haploblocks:
#1: select the top n blocks based on Block_Var
#2: select the top x% of blocks (round up)
#3: select the top blocks explaining x% of the total sum of block variance (round up)


#1: select top 15 haploblocks (arbitrary)

haploblock_obj = select_top_blocks(haploblock_obj = haploblock_obj, n = 15) #n denotes the number of blocks
#Objects are added to the haploblock_obj for the GA


#2 select top 50% of haploblocks
haploblock_obj = select_top_blocks(haploblock_obj = haploblock_obj, perc_total = 0.5) #perc_total is the percentage of blocks to select (rounded up)

#3 select the top blocks explaining at least 90% of the total block variance
haploblock_obj = select_top_blocks(haploblock_obj = haploblock_obj, perc_of_total_var = 0.9) #perc_of_total_var is the proportion of blocks exlaining at lest a given threshold of the total block variation (rounded up)

#select the same blocks for the haplotype effects
haplotype_obj = select_top_blocks(haploblock_obj = haplotype_obj, perc_of_total_var = 0.9)

#Parent Selection (localGEBV)
localGEBV_parent_obj = local_gebv_parent_selection(
    haploblock_obj = haploblock_obj,    #haploblock object from select_top_blocks() computed using compute_local_GEBV()
    n_founders = 20,                    #number of parents to select
    popSize = 10,                       #parameter to aid optimization - higher uses more memory and each iteration is slower, but leads to faster convergence
    maxiter = 300,                      #max number of iterations
    run = 150,                          #max number of iterations of no change before termination
    pmutation = 0.6,                    #probability of swapping one idividual randomly in a population each iteration - aids in parameter space exploration
    pcrossover = 0.6,                   #probability of exchanging members between two populations in each iteration - aids in parameter space exploration
    maximize = TRUE,                    #if TRUE, maximise potential GEBV, if FALSE, minimise
    monitor = TRUE,                     #if TRUE, print out optimisation statisitcs each iteration
    strategy = "no_selfing"             #"no_selfing" does not allow selfing in optimisation (i.e., two distinct parents per block) whereas "selfing" does allow the same parent to be utilized twice per block
)

#Parent Selection (haplotypes - diploid only!)
haplotype_parent_obj = haplotype_parent_selection(
    haploblock_obj = haplotype_obj,     #haploblock object from select_top_blocks() computed using compute_haplotype_effects()
    n_founders = 20,                    #number of parents to select
    popSize = 10,                       #parameter to aid optimization - higher uses more memory and each iteration is slower, but leads to faster convergence
    maxiter = 300,                      #max number of iterations
    run = 150,                          #max number of iterations of no change before termination
    pmutation = 0.6,                    #probability of swapping one idividual randomly in a population each iteration - aids in parameter space exploration

    maximize = TRUE,                    #if TRUE, maximize potential GEBV, if FALSE, minimize
    monitor = TRUE,                     #if TRUE, print out optimisation statisitcs each iteration
    strategy = "OHS"                    #"OHS" enforces haplotypes must come from two different parents, "OPV" allows the same haplotype to be utilised twice, "Haploid_OHS" allows the same parent to contribute two haplotypes, but not from the same chromosome
)

localGEBV_parent_obj$selected_founders #substitute haplotype_parent_obj for haplotypes

plot(localGEBV_parent_obj$GA)

If strategy is not specified, the GA functions use the least constrained strategy ("selfing" for localGEBV, "OPV" for haplotypes). See Parent Selection.

docs.title: Process Overview
docs.text: HapSelect implements a six-stage pipeline that moves from raw genotype/allelic data to aggregated genomic signals in the form of haplotype effects/localGEBV and haplotype catalogues, and finally to an optimised set of founder parents for a genomic selection program.

docs.title: A — Block Formation
docs.text:
The first stage partitions the genome into haplotype blocks (haploblocks) using linkage disequilibrium (LD) between markers or a window-based approach. We highly recommend using our internal LD tool written in C++ or PLINK 1.9 to compute pairwise LD. If PLINK 1.9 is installed (see Installation and Configuration), we offer a wrapper function to compute LD and format the output appropriately with the plink_pairwise_ld_geno() function. See Pairwise LD for more information.

LD-Based Blocking: Starting from a map and pared-down VCF structured genotype/allelic matrix of N individuals × I markers (localGEBV) or IL Chromosomes (Haplotypes), where I and L are the number of markers and ploidy (see Pairwise LD for more details), HapSelect:

  1. Computes pairwise r² between all marker pairs within each chromosome
  2. Uses the r² matrix to define contiguous regions of high internal LD — haploblocks

The result is a set of J haploblocks that tile the genome, each capturing a segment of genetic co-variation. Haploblock IDs follow the convention of Chromosome:Block, identifying blocks nested within chromosome.

A custom haploblock dataframe can be provided, but it must follow the output structure produced from block_obj_to_df().

Window-Based Blocking: Starting from a map, HapSelect will group markers from left (start of a chromosome) to right. Grouping occurs by either physical/genetic distance in the map, or a specified number of markers - whichever is specified. No LD is required.

Graph-Based Blocking: Graph-based blocking is a new implementation and is similar in concept to LD based blocking. Starting from a map and pared-down VCF structured genotype matrix of N individuals × I markers, HapSelect will:

  1. Compute pairwise r² between all marker pairs within each chromosome
  2. Compute core marker connections between markers to form seed regions based on high LD
  3. Extend core marker connections and bridge cores based on lower LD connections
  4. Linearise the proto-blocks because they often overlap
  5. Refill markers that were not placed

Because LD is computed within a short window of each marker, graph-based blocking computes the LD it needs internally from the genotype matrix and does not require a pairwise LD table. See Haplotype Blocks for diagrams of each strategy.

#### LD-Based Blocking ####

#compute pairwise LD

#R implementation using a C++ backend
ld_pairs   <- pairwise_ld(
  genotype_matrix = geno,
  parallelize     = FALSE,
  window          = NULL,
  min_r2          = NULL,
  min_obs         = 2L
)

#PLINK backend
ld_pairs   <- plink_pairwise_ld_geno(
  geno           = geno,
  ld_window      = 999999,
  ld_window_kb   = 1e6,
  ld_window_r2   = 0
)

#make a haploblock list object
haploblocks <- def_blocks(
  map         = map,
  strategy    = ld_strategy(
    ld        = ld_pairs,
    method    = "flanking",
    tolerance = 3,
    threshold = 0.5,
    start     = "beginning",
    tol_reset = TRUE,
    parallel  = FALSE
  )
)

#### Window-Based Blocking #####

#make a haploblock list object

#using fixed physical distance of cM widths, depending on the map
haploblocks <- def_blocks(
  map         = map,
  strategy    = window_strategy(
    window    = 100000, # 100kb window
    method    = "window_map"
  )
)

#using fixed SNP intervals
haploblocks <- def_blocks(
  map         = map,
  strategy    = window_strategy(
    window    = 50, # every 50 SNP
    method    = "window_snp"
  )
)

#### Graph-Based Blocking ####

#LD calculated internally - geno is required
haploblocks <- def_blocks(
  map          = map,
  geno         = geno,
  strategy     = graph_strategy(
    theta_core        = 0.80,
    theta_core_by_chr = NULL,
    theta_extend      = 0.20,
    theta_bridge      = 0.20,
    theta_refill      = 0.80,
    ld_min_r2         = 0.20,
    window_ld         = 20,
    window_core       = 20,
    window_extend     = 50,
    min_links         = 1,
    max_gap_snps      = 2,
    max_gap_markers   = 2,
    max_gap_position  = NULL,
    min_block_snps    = 2,
    parallel          = FALSE
  )
)

#### turn the list object into a singular data frame #####

# All methods:
haploblocks <- block_obj_to_df(haploblocks, map = map)

Tip

There are many parameters that affect the behaviour of different strategy within def_blocks() with various defaults. Be sure to check out all options and how they can influence the result. See Haplotype Blocks for more details!

docs.title: B — SNP Effect Estimation
docs.text:
Marker effects are estimated independently using a genomic prediction model — GBLUP with backsolve, BayesR, rrBLUP, other Bayesian methods, or any equivalent method that produces per-SNP effect estimates (\(\hat{\alpha}_m\)).

HapSelect offers a basic genomic prediction model (dosage genotype matrix only in localGEBV) by integrating the rrBLUP R Package. However, the implementation is limited to utilising singular BLUE, adjusted phenotype, or deregressed BLUP for each individual and no other effects may be included in the model. For any users needing to employ more advanced modelling, please consult the packages below.

Any model that returns a vector of marker effect estimates aligned to the same map can be used and it is up to the user to ensure marker effect estimates are correctly generated. Please see localGEBV for file structure details.

docs.title: Example R Packages for Genomic Prediction:
docs.text:
SNP Based Models: rrBLUP BGLR Sommer ASREML-R

GBLUP Based Models: rrBLUP Sommer ASREML-R

# Example using rrBLUP integration into package
marker_effects <- create_marker_effects_file(geno = geno, BLUE = BLUE, h2_method = "VanRaden", ploidy = 2L)

docs.title: C — LocalGEBV / Haplotype Effects
docs.text:
With haploblocks defined and marker effects estimated, HapSelect calculates a local genomic estimated breeding value (localGEBV) for each individual in each haploblock:

\[ \text{localGEBV}_{jk} = \sum_{i \in \text{block}_j} ({x_{ik}} - \overline{x_{i}}) \cdot \hat{\alpha}_i \]

where \(({x_{ik}} - \overline{x_{i}})\) is the centered (see Van Raden, 2008) allele dosage of individual \(k\) at marker \(i\) in haploblock \(j\), and \(\hat{\alpha}_i\) is the estimated marker effect.

This produces an \(\text{J × N}\) matrix of localGEBV values — one value per individual for \(N\) individuals per haploblock for \(J\) haploblocks — which captures the breeding value contribution of each genomic region separately.

#localGEBV
haploblock_obj <- compute_local_GEBV(
  geno           = geno,
  marker_effects = marker_effects,
  haploblocks_df = haploblocks,
  set_missing_NA = TRUE,            #if TRUE, any missing genotypes in a block will return NA for the localGEBV
  mean_adjust    = TRUE             #centeres the genotype matrix - this should be TRUE in almost every case! Setting to FALSE will lead to biased localGEBV!
)

#haplotypes
haplotype_obj <- compute_haplotype_effects(
  geno           = geno_phased,
  marker_effects = marker_effects,
  haploblocks_df = haploblocks,
  set_missing_NA = TRUE,            #if TRUE, any missing alleles in a block will return NA for the haplotype effect
  mean_adjust    = TRUE             #centeres the allele matrix - this should be TRUE in almost every case! Setting to FALSE will lead to biased haplotype effects!
)

Haplotype effects are similarly generated:

\[ \text{Haplotype}_{jkl} = \sum_{i \in \text{block}_j} ({x_{ikl}} - \frac{\overline{x_{i}}}{2}) \cdot \hat{\alpha}_i \]

where all terms are the same, except \(({x_{ikl}} - \frac{\overline{x_{i}}}{2})\) is the centered allele of individual \(k\) on chromosome \(l\) at marker \(i\) in haploblock \(j\) and the result is the haplotype effect of individual \(k\) for chromosome \(l\) and haploblock \(j\). The centered allele is equivalent to subtracting the allele frequency, p, from the allele in 0/1 format. Dividing the mean dosage by 2 is equivalent for a diploid where the mean is 2p.

This produces an \(\text{J × NL}\) matrix of haplotype effects — one value per individual per chromosome for \(L\) chromosome sets per haploblock for \(J\) haploblocks.

docs.title: D — Haploblock Variance
docs.text:
Not all haploblocks are equally informative. HapSelect ranks blocks by the variance of localGEBV/haplotype effects across individuals:

\[ \text{var}(\mathbf{\text{localGEBV}_j}) = \frac{\sum_i \left( \text{localGEBV}_{ij} - \overline{\text{localGEBV}_j} \right)^2}{N} \]

where \(\text{var}(\mathbf{\text{localGEBV}_j})\) is the haploblock variance. Similarly for haplotypes, variance is computed with haplotype effects instead of localGEBV

High-variance blocks are those where individuals differ substantially in their localGEBV/haplotype effects — these are the genomic regions where parent choice will have the greatest impact on offspring breeding value.

The funnel plots visualise this across all blocks, with localGEBV/haplotype effects on the x-axis and block variance on the y-axis scaled using a 0 to 1 min-max scaling procedure. Similarly, localGEBV/haplotype effects can be visualised in a Manhattan-style plot (for more details and information, see Visualisations).

docs.title: E and F — Haploblock and Parent Selection
docs.text:
The top-ranked haploblocks (by variance) are used as targets for the genetic algorithm. local_gebv_parent_selection()/haplotype_parent_selection() searches for a set of n_founders parents that collectively carry the highest-value localGEBV/haplotype alleles across the selected blocks, subject to constraints on crossing scheme and population size.

#1: select top 15 haploblocks (arbitrary)
haploblock_obj <- select_top_blocks(haploblock_obj = haploblock_obj, n = 15)

#2 select top 50% of haploblocks (arbitrary)
haploblock_obj <- select_top_blocks(haploblock_obj = haploblock_obj, perc_total = 0.5)

#3 select the top blocks explaining at least 90% of the total block variance (arbitrary)
haploblock_obj <- select_top_blocks(haploblock_obj = haploblock_obj, perc_of_total_var = 0.9)

#Parent Selection (localGEBV)
localGEBV_parent_obj = local_gebv_parent_selection(
    haploblock_obj   = haploblock_obj, 
    n_founders       = 20,                    
    popSize          = 10,                       
    strategy         = "no_selfing"             
)

#Parent Selection (haplotypes - diploid only!)
haplotype_obj <- select_top_blocks(haploblock_obj = haplotype_obj, perc_of_total_var = 0.9)

haplotype_parent_obj = haplotype_parent_selection(
    haploblock_obj   = haplotype_obj,
    n_founders       = 20,                    
    popSize          = 10,                       
    strategy         = "OHS"                    
)

Tip

There are many parameters that affect the behaviour of the genetic algorithm parent selection functions and convergence to an optimal solution with various defaults. Be sure to check out all options and how they can influence the result. See Parent Selection for full parameter details!

docs.title: G — Basic Simulation and Parental Diversity
docs.text:
The parents selected by the genetic algorithm (GA) and the parents selected by truncation selection (TS; i.e., best whole-genome GEBV) can be utilised in a basic simulation using recurrent TS for each set of parents to compare genetic gain over time. We have provided a wrapper for the genomicSimulation R package (Villiers et al., 2022) to conduct the simulation and plot the rate of genetic gain based on each set of parents. Furthermore, we also offer an option to conduct principal component analysis (PCA) and return a PCA dataframe as well as a PCA plot for the first two PC that maps where each set of parents and their overlap sit in the overall population diversity. The whole-genome GEBV of the GA parents and TS parents (calculated internally) are then utilised to perform the simulation.

For more information on parameters, see Basic Simulation.

#Basic Recurrent Truncation Selection Simulation and Diversity Analysis (haplotypes)
Haplotype_Sim = Haplotype_vs_TS_simulation(
    GA_output      = haplotype_parent_obj,
    geno_phased    = geno_phased,                                    
    marker_effects = marker_effects,                       
    map            = map
)

#Basic Recurrent Truncation Selection Simulation and Diversity Analysis (localGEBV)
localGEBV_Sim = localGEBV_vs_TS_simulation(
    GA_output      = localGEBV_parent_obj,
    geno           = geno,                                           
    marker_effects = marker_effects,                       
    map            = map
)

Tip

There are many parameters that affect the behaviour of localGEBV_vs_TS_simulation() and Haplotype_vs_TS_simulation(). Be sure to check out all options and how they can influence the result. See Basic Simulation for full parameter details!

docs.title: Progress Reporting
docs.text:
Many HapSelect steps take minutes to hours on real datasets. HapSelect reports what it is doing and how far along it is in one of two ways:

  • Progress bars (default) - one labelled bar per step, for people watching an R session or terminal.
  • Machine-readable events - one JSON line per event on stderr, for other programs (pipelines, dashboards, web front ends) to follow a run. See Machine-Readable Progress.

Progress reporting never changes any results.

docs.title: Progress Bars
docs.text:
Progress bars from LD calculation through to simulation on the example data (sped up).

Every long-running function reports as a named step with its own bar. The text beside a bar says what the step is currently doing (e.g., Fold 3/5, Building blocks, or the genetic algorithm's current fitness). Work that cannot be counted, such as waiting on BEAGLE to start, shows a spinner with the time taken. A step that stops with an error marks its bar as failed.

Bars are drawn when R is running interactively (e.g., RStudio) or in a terminal. When output is redirected to a file, as in most batch jobs, bars are switched off automatically and the same information is printed as plain text instead (for example, the genetic algorithm prints one line per iteration when monitor = TRUE).

Tip

While a bar is being drawn, anything a step prints (such as the variance components printed for each cross-validation fold) is held back and printed once the step finishes, so it does not break up the bar. Nothing is lost.

docs.title: Turning progress bars off
docs.text:
#for the rest of the session
options(progressr.enable = FALSE)

Or, before starting R (e.g., for a scheduled job), set the environment variable R_PROGRESSR_ENABLE=false.

docs.title: Other settings
docs.text: Setting Default Description options(HapSelect.progress_interval = ) 0.2 Minimum number of seconds between progress updates. Must be set before HapSelect is loaded (e.g., in your .Rprofile) options(cli.progress_show_after = ) 0 Seconds before a bar is shown options(cli.progress_clear = ) FALSE If TRUE, finished bars are removed instead of left on screen

docs.title: Using your own progress handler
docs.text:
HapSelect reports progress through the progressr package. If you have already set your own handlers with progressr::handlers() (e.g., in your .Rprofile) before HapSelect is loaded, HapSelect leaves them alone. You can also replace HapSelect's handler at any time:

progressr::handlers("txtprogressbar")

Other handlers still show progress, but not the step names or status text, which only HapSelect's own handler knows about.

docs.title: Machine-Readable Progress
docs.text:
Setting the environment variable HAPSELECT_MACHINE_LOGGING=1 before HapSelect is loaded replaces the progress bars with a stream of events on stderr, one JSON object per line:

HAPSELECT_MACHINE_LOGGING=1 Rscript my_analysis.R

@@HS {"v":"2.0.0","at":"2026-11-02T04:14:18.374Z","event":"step_started","step":"window_blocking","label":"Window Blocking"}
@@HS {"v":"2.0.0","at":"2026-11-02T04:14:18.385Z","event":"progress","step":"window_blocking","current":0,"total":21}
@@HS {"v":"2.0.0","at":"2026-11-02T04:14:18.390Z","event":"progress","step":"window_blocking","current":21,"total":21}
@@HS {"v":"2.0.0","at":"2026-11-02T04:14:18.391Z","event":"step_finished","step":"window_blocking","status":"succeeded"}

Nothing else about a run changes: results, printed output, warnings, and errors are the same as without it.

docs.title: Reading the stream
docs.text:
• Every event line starts with the prefix @@HS (including the trailing space). Warnings, messages, and output from PLINK and BEAGLE share stderr, so keep only lines that start with the prefix and parse the rest of the line as JSON.
  • Fields with no value are left out rather than sent as null.
  • Numbers are written in full precision.
  • Progress events are throttled to at most one every HapSelect.progress_interval seconds (0.2 by default), so not every increment is sent. Use current and total rather than counting events.

docs.title: Common fields
docs.text:
Every event has:

Field Type Description v string Protocol version, which is the installed HapSelect version (e.g., "2.0.0") at string Time the event was sent, ISO 8601 in UTC with milliseconds (e.g., "2026-11-02T04:14:18.374Z") event string "step_started", "progress", "step_finished", or "metric"

docs.title: Example: following a run from Python
docs.text:
import json
import os
import subprocess

env = dict(os.environ, HAPSELECT_MACHINE_LOGGING="1")
proc = subprocess.Popen(["Rscript", "my_analysis.R"], env=env,
                        stderr=subprocess.PIPE, text=True)

steps = []  #a stack, because steps can nest
for line in proc.stderr:
    if not line.startswith("@@HS "):
        continue  #a warning, message, or PLINK/BEAGLE output
    event = json.loads(line[len("@@HS "):])

    if event["event"] == "step_started":
        steps.append(event["step"])
        print("started:", event["label"])
    elif event["event"] == "step_finished":
        steps.remove(event["step"])
        print("finished:", event["step"], event["status"], event.get("message", ""))
    elif event["event"] == "progress" and "total" in event:
        print(f"  {event['step']}: {event['current']}/{event['total']}")
    elif event["event"] == "metric":
        print("  metric:", event["name"], event["values"])

proc.wait()

Tip

With machine logging on, progress is reported even when R is not interactive, so it works under Rscript, job schedulers, and subprocesses. Setting R_PROGRESSR_ENABLE=false as well stops the progress events, but step_started, step_finished, and metric events are still sent.

docs.title: Basic GA vs TS Simulation
docs.text:
The localGEBV_vs_TS_simulation() and Haplotype_vs_TS_simulation() functions perform a simplified recurrent genomic selection simulation comparing:

  • parents selected using the HapSelect genetic algorithm (GA) with localGEBV or haplotype effects
  • parents selected using standard genomic truncation selection (TS)

The simulation evaluates long-term breeding value trajectories across generations and can optionally visualise population structure using PCA to demonstrate where parents are being sourced.

docs.title: Advantages of GA vs TS
docs.text:
In general, if a population has been under selection for a given trait, the best parents identified by whole-genome GEBV via TS tend to be related. In other words, they're good because they share the same good genomic segements; but conversely, they also share the same bad genomic segments. The GA with the default fitness functions, in comparison, will attempt to match indviduals by potential contribution. This necessarily means individuals tend to be less related if the population has been under selection for the given trait. This also means genetic variance tends to be greater in these individuals, even if the mean GEBV of the GA parents is initially worse than the TS parents. Thus, long-term selection potential is usually greater. This simulation attempts to demonstrate that diversity potential.

In the PCA, GA, TS, and overlapping parents are marked for visualisation. If the TS-selected parents tend to cluster to a small region of the PCA plot, it usually means that trait has been under selection in that population and such a scenario is where GA-selected parents shine. However, if TS are dispersed and thus unrelated, then realised differences between the GA and TS-selected parents tend to be minimal or even unfavourable.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The simulation performs the following steps:

  1. Extracts GA-selected parents from the GA output object (haplotype_parent_selection() or local_gebv_parent_selection() functions)
  2. Selects TS parents based on highest GEBV
  3. Converts physical marker positions to proportional genetic positions in cM (if needed)
  4. Simulates recurrent random crossing and selection across generations
  5. Repeats the simulation multiple times to quantify Monte Carlo variability
  6. Summarises breeding value trajectories
  7. Generates trajectory and PCA visualisations of selected parents

The simulation is intentionally simple and designed primarily for:

  • comparing parent selection strategies
  • evaluating long-term gain potential
  • exploring diversity retention
  • demonstrating GA optimisation behaviour

docs.title: Running the Simulation
docs.text:
#localGEBV
localGEBV_Sim  <- localGEBV_vs_TS_simulation(
  GA_output            = localGEBV_parent_obj,
  geno                 = geno,
  marker_effects       = marker_effects,
  map                  = map,
  genetic_map_position = NULL,
  num_gen              = 50,
  num_sim_reps         = 30,
  num_cross_per_gen    = 1000,
  num_TS_parents       = NULL,
  mean_adjust          = TRUE,
  maximize             = TRUE,
  max_cM_chr           = 100,
  PCA                  = TRUE,
  colors               = c("green", "#d95f02", "#A01FF0", "gray80"),
  alpha                = c(1,1,1,0.5)
)

#Haplotype
Haplotype_Sim  <- Haplotype_vs_TS_simulation(
  GA_output            = haplotype_parent_obj,
  geno_phased          = geno_phased,
  marker_effects       = marker_effects,
  map                  = map,
  genetic_map_position = NULL,
  num_gen              = 50,
  num_sim_reps         = 30,
  num_cross_per_gen    = 1000,
  num_TS_parents       = NULL,
  mean_adjust          = TRUE,
  maximize             = TRUE,

  PCA                  = TRUE,
  colors               = c("green", "#d95f02", "#A01FF0", "gray80"),
  alpha                = c(1,1,1,0.5)
)

docs.title: 1. Marker Compatibility Checks
docs.text:
The function internally verifies that:

  • marker IDs match between geno, marker_effects, and map
  • marker IDs contain no duplicates
  • marker IDs contain no missing values

The simulation will stop immediately if incompatibilities are detected.

docs.title: 2. GEBV Calculation
docs.text:
The function computes genomic estimated breeding values (GEBV) using:

GEBV = Zu

where:

  • Z is the genotype matrix
  • u is the marker effect vector

If mean_adjust = TRUE, markers are internally centered before GEBV calculation.

This should remain TRUE in almost all analyses, but in practice will not affect the simulation because it will not change GEBV ranking.

docs.title: 3. TS Parent Selection
docs.text:
Truncation-selected parents are chosen as the individuals with the highest (or lowest when maximize = FALSE GEBV values.

Example:

num_TS_parents = 20

selects the top 20 individuals ranked by GEBV.

If num_TS_parents = NULL, the number of TS parents automatically matches the number of GA parents.

docs.title: 4. Genetic Map Construction
docs.text:
The simulation requires marker positions in centiMorgans (cM).

Two approaches are supported.

docs.title: Using a True Genetic Map (Recommended)
docs.text:
#example of how to supply the genetic map positions
genetic_map_position = map$cM

The vector must:

  • be the same length as map
  • contain no missing values
  • be in the same marker order as map

This is the most biologically realistic option.

docs.title: Inferring Genetic Positions from Physical Distance
docs.text:
If:

genetic_map_position = NULL

then marker positions are inferred proportionally from physical distance relative to the first and last marker positions (i.e., the first marker is 0 cM and the last is 100 cM with the rest based on proportion of distance between the first and last marker).

Each chromosome is assumed to span:

max_cM_chr = 100

by default.

Example:

max_cM_chr = 150

would assume each chromosome spans 150 cM.

docs.title: Recurrent Selection Simulation
docs.text:
The simulation uses the genomicSimulation package internally.

For each generation:

  1. Mean breeding value is recorded
  2. Top individuals are selected by GEBV
  3. Random crosses generate the next generation
  4. The process repeats for num_gen generations

This procedure is independently repeated num_sim_reps times for each set of parents to quantify stochastic simulation variability. While the simulation runs, the progress bar shows which set of parents and replicate is being simulated (e.g., GA parents | rep 3/30), see Progress Reporting. Variability is derived from recombination differences, random mating sampling, Mendelian sampling (random inheritance), and, in the case of unphased data, random phasing of heterozygotes initially.

docs.title: num_gen
docs.text: Controls the number of recurrent selection generations.

docs.title: Larger Values
docs.text:
• better evaluate long-term gain
  • reveal selection plateaus
  • better assess diversity preservation

docs.title: Smaller Values
docs.text:
• faster simulations
  • emphasize short-term gain

docs.title: num_sim_reps
docs.text:
Controls the number of independent simulation replicates.

Replicates differ because of:

  • recombination randomness
  • stochastic inheritance
  • random mating patterns
  • random phasing (if using dosage heterozygotes)

docs.title: Larger Values
docs.text:
Advantages:

  • smoother trajectories
  • reduced stochastic noise
  • more stable estimates

Disadvantages:

  • slower runtime
  • increased memory usage

docs.title: num_cross_per_gen
docs.text: Controls the number of progeny generated each generation.

docs.title: Larger Values
docs.text:
Advantages:

  • stronger selection intensity
  • greater opportunity for favourable recombination
  • smoother trajectories
  • more stable representation of genomic variability (i.e., less drift)

Disadvantages:

  • slower simulations
  • increased memory usage

docs.title: mean_adjust
docs.text:
Controls genotype centering before GEBV calculation.

Recommended setting:

mean_adjust = TRUE

This should only be disabled if you know what you are doing! However, in practice, it affects very little in this step.

Warning

Centering is currently not conducted in GenomicSimulation simulations - therefore, BV may be mean shifted!

docs.title: PCA
docs.text:
If TRUE, PCA is performed on the genotype matrix.

The PCA visualisation highlights:

  • GA-selected parents
  • TS-selected parents
  • overlapping parents
  • non-selected individuals

This helps visualise:

  • diversity retention
  • population structure
  • overlap between strategies
  • presence of selection pressure

docs.title: PCA Plot Colors
docs.text:
The colors argument must contain exactly four valid R colors in the following order:

colors = c(
  "green",
  "#d95f02",
  "#A01FF0",
  "gray80"
)
Position Meaning 1 GA-selected parents 2 TS-selected parents 3 Individuals selected by both methods 4 Non-selected individuals

Tip

Even if PCA = FALSE, this should still be specified with 4 colors as the first two are utilised simultaneously for the Simulation_Plot

docs.title: PCA Transparency
docs.text:
The alpha argument controls point transparency on the PCA plot.

alpha = c(1,1,1,0.5)
Position Meaning 1 GA-selected parents 2 TS-selected parents 3 Overlapping parents 4 Non-selected individuals

All values must be between:

0 and 1

If PCA = FALSE, only Simulation_Plot and Simulation_Summary are returned.
