docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Simulations utilise random mating
  • Selection each generation occurs entirely on GEBV (TS)
  • Missing genotype values are internally replaced prior to simulation (currently as heterozygous and randomly phased by GenomicSimulation)
  • Temporary files are written to R's temporary directory (tempdir()) and deleted automatically, so nothing is left in your working directory
  • Simulations are stochastic and results will vary slightly between runs
  • Imputing before beginning HapSelect and providing a phased input for simulation (haplotype genotype matrix and function call, even if parent selection was with localGEBV) will reduce some of the stochastic behavior between runs

docs.title: Data Import, Imputation, and Phasing
docs.text:
HapSelect can read genotypes straight from a VCF file, and impute and phase them with BEAGLE 5.5, so that the genotype matrix (geno, localGEBV) and phased genotype matrix (geno_phased, haplotypes) can be produced without leaving R.

Function Input Output read_vcf_geno() VCF file Dosage genotype matrix (geno) read_vcf_phased() Phased VCF file Phased genotype matrix (geno_phased) beagle_impute_geno() geno with missing values Imputed geno beagle_phase_geno() geno Imputed and phased geno_phased beagle_impute() VCF file Imputed and phased VCF file center_genotypes() geno or geno_phased Centered genotypes

See Getting Started for the structure of the genotype and phased genotype matrices.

Warning

The VCF functions do not currently handle aneuploidy or variable ploidy - every genotype call in a file must have the same number of alleles. BEAGLE, and therefore every beagle_*() function, only supports diploid genotypes.

docs.title: read_vcf_geno()
docs.text:
Reads a VCF file (.vcf or gzipped .vcf.gz) into a dosage genotype matrix: the number of alternative (ALT) alleles at each marker for each individual.

geno <- read_vcf_geno(
  path      = "path/to/genotypes.vcf.gz",
  prefer_ds = FALSE,              #if TRUE, read imputed dosages from the DS field instead of GT
  ploidy    = 2L                  #number of alleles per genotype call
)
Parameter Default Description path Path to a .vcf or .vcf.gz file prefer_ds FALSE Read dosages from the DS field instead of GT ploidy 2L Number of alleles in every genotype call. Dosages run from 0 to ploidy

The result has the SNP (from the VCF ID column), Chromosome, and Position columns followed by one column per sample.

  • Phased (0|1) and unphased (0/1) calls are both read.
  • A call with any missing allele (./., 0/.) becomes NA.
  • A call with a second ALT allele (e.g., 1/2) is an error, because a single ALT count cannot express it. Split multi-allelic sites into biallelic markers before reading (e.g., with bcftools norm -m -).
  • A call with a different number of alleles to ploidy is an error.

prefer_ds

  • FALSE -> dosages are the hard calls from GT (whole numbers).
  • TRUE -> dosages are read from the DS field, which imputation software (including BEAGLE with a reference panel) writes alongside GT. These are fractional (e.g., 0.83 rather than 1), keeping the imputation's uncertainty. If any record lacks DS, the whole file is read from GT instead.

Warning

Fractional dosages from prefer_ds = TRUE work with pairwise_ld() and all haploblocking strategies, but cannot be written to PLINK format, so they will not work with plink_pairwise_ld_geno()!

Tip

Chromosomes are read as they are written in the VCF (e.g., "1A", "chr2"). Run order_map() and order_geno() on the result to number the chromosomes and sort the markers before using it anywhere else:

geno <- read_vcf_geno("path/to/genotypes.vcf.gz")
map  <- order_map(geno[, 1:3], verbose = TRUE)
geno <- order_geno(geno, map)

docs.title: read_vcf_phased()
docs.text:
Reads a phased VCF file into the phased genotype matrix used for haplotype effects. Each sample's call is split into one column per chromosome copy (sample_1, sample_2, ...) of 0 (REF) / 1 (ALT) alleles.

geno_phased <- read_vcf_phased(
  path   = "path/to/phased.vcf.gz",
  ploidy = 2L
)
Parameter Default Description path Path to a phased .vcf or .vcf.gz file ploidy 2L Number of alleles in every genotype call

Warning

Every call must be fully phased (| between every allele) with no missing alleles, because each allele has to be placed on a chromosome copy. An unphased (0/1) or missing (.|.) call is an error naming the sample - phase and impute the genotypes first (e.g., with beagle_phase_geno()), or use read_vcf_geno() to read the file as dosages.

docs.title: Imputation and Phasing with BEAGLE
docs.text:
The beagle_*() functions run BEAGLE 5.5 for you. BEAGLE always phases, and phasing fills in missing genotypes as it goes, so a single BEAGLE run both phases and imputes. The functions only differ in what they read and return.

Warning

BEAGLE 5.5 and a Java runtime (Java 8 or later) MUST be installed to use these functions. HapSelect looks for a beagle*.jar file in the install scripts' ~/bin folder, then in every folder on the system PATH, and only accepts BEAGLE 5.5. Use set_beagle_path() to point HapSelect at a specific .jar file (see Configuration). See Installation for more details.

All three functions share the following optional parameters:

Parameter Default Description ref NULL Path to a reference panel VCF for reference-based imputation (Optional) map NULL Path to a PLINK-format genetic map, passed to BEAGLE's map= argument. This is not the HapSelect map data frame! (Optional) extra_args character() Additional BEAGLE key=value arguments, e.g., c("ne=100", "window=40")

Tip

Without ref, BEAGLE imputes missing genotypes from the samples in your own data. A reference panel is only needed to impute markers that are absent from your data, or to improve accuracy with a larger, related population. Without map, BEAGLE assumes a constant recombination rate of 1 cM per Mb.

Tip

BEAGLE is limited to the number of cores allowed by set_cpu_cores(). To override this for a single call, pass nthreads= in extra_args, e.g., extra_args = c("nthreads=4").

docs.title: beagle_phase_geno()
docs.text:
Imputes and phases a dosage genotype matrix, returning the phased genotype matrix (geno_phased) that compute_haplotype_effects() expects.

geno_phased <- beagle_phase_geno(
  geno       = geno,
  ref        = NULL,
  map        = NULL,
  extra_args = character()
)

docs.title: beagle_impute_geno()
docs.text:
Imputes missing genotypes in a dosage genotype matrix and returns a dosage genotype matrix in the same layout, sample order, and sample names as geno.

geno_imputed <- beagle_impute_geno(
  geno       = geno,
  ref        = NULL,
  map        = NULL,
  extra_args = character(),
  prefer_ds  = FALSE
)
Parameter Default Description prefer_ds FALSE If TRUE, return BEAGLE's fractional imputed dosages (DS) instead of hard calls. See read_vcf_geno() above

Warning

BEAGLE only writes DS when imputing against a reference panel. prefer_ds = TRUE without ref has no effect and produces a warning.

Tip

beagle_impute_geno() discards the phasing BEAGLE produced, because a dosage cannot express which chromosome an allele sits on. If you need both a dosage matrix (localGEBV) and a phased matrix (haplotypes) from the same imputation, run beagle_phase_geno() and sum each individual's two chromosome columns to get dosages.

For both beagle_phase_geno() and beagle_impute_geno(), geno must be diploid (dosages of 0, 1, 2, or NA).

docs.title: beagle_impute()
docs.text:
Runs BEAGLE on a VCF file directly and writes the imputed and phased result to <out_prefix>.vcf.gz. Use this when your data is already in VCF format or too large to hold comfortably in R.

out_vcf <- beagle_impute(
  vcf_in     = "path/to/genotypes.vcf.gz",
  out_prefix = "path/to/imputed",          #BEAGLE writes path/to/imputed.vcf.gz and path/to/imputed.log
  ref        = NULL,
  map        = NULL,
  extra_args = character()
)

#read the result back in
geno_phased <- read_vcf_phased(out_vcf)

beagle_impute() returns the path to the output VCF.

docs.title: center_genotypes()
docs.text:
Centers a genotype (or phased genotype) matrix by subtracting each marker's mean from every individual. Missing values are ignored when calculating the mean and remain NA.

geno_centered <- center_genotypes(geno = geno)

Tip

You do not need to center genotypes yourself before computing localGEBV or haplotype effects - compute_local_GEBV() and compute_haplotype_effects() do this internally with mean_adjust = TRUE. center_genotypes() is provided for custom analyses outside the HapSelect workflow.

docs.title: HapSelect Workflow Tutorial
docs.text:
This tutorial demonstrates a complete HapSelect workflow, including:

  1. Preparing genotype and map files (and, optionally, importing, imputing, and phasing a VCF file)
  2. Computing linkage disequilibrium (LD)
  3. Constructing haploblocks with LD-based, window-based, or graph-based blocking
  4. Estimating marker effects
  5. Computing localGEBV/haplotype effects
  6. Visualizing haploblocks, marker effects, localGEBV, haploblock variance, LD decay, and more
  7. Parent selection with the genetic algorithm (GA)
  8. Simulating recurrent truncation selection (TS) with GA selected parents vs TS selected parents

Each step links to its own page with the full parameter documentation.

docs.title: Loading Example Data
docs.text:
HapSelect ships with several small example datasets:

  • map
  • geno
  • geno_phased
  • ld_pairs
  • BLUE
  • marker_effects
library(HapSelect)

map            <- HapSelect::map
geno           <- HapSelect::geno
geno_phased    <- HapSelect::geno_phased
BLUE           <- HapSelect::BLUE

docs.title: Map File
docs.text:
The map file must contain:

Column Description SNP Character marker/SNP identifier Chromosome Numeric chromosome identifier Position Numeric physical position or genetic map position

Example:

head(HapSelect::map)

docs.title: Genotype File
docs.text:
The genotype file should contain:

Columns Description First 3 columns Map information (SNP, Chromosome, Position) in the same order and format Remaining columns Individuals/accessions genotypes with the column name denoting the individual

Genotypes are expected to be numeric dosage coded:

  • Diploid: usually 0/1/2
  • Polyploid: supports up to any integer ploidy

Or, when performing a true haplotype analysis, 0/1 only with L columns per individual representing a ploidy of L

Missing values should be:

NA

Example:

head(HapSelect::geno[,1:10])
head(HapSelect::geno_phased[,1:10])

docs.title: Importing Your Own Data from a VCF File (Optional)
docs.text:
If your genotypes are in a VCF file, they can be read directly into the format above. If they need imputing or phasing (required for haplotype effects), BEAGLE 5.5 can be run from R. See Data Import, Imputation, and Phasing for all options.

#read dosages and number/sort the chromosomes
geno <- read_vcf_geno("path/to/genotypes.vcf.gz")
map  <- order_map(geno[, 1:3], verbose = TRUE)
geno <- order_geno(geno, map)

#impute and phase with BEAGLE (requires BEAGLE 5.5 and Java)
geno_phased <- beagle_phase_geno(geno)

Tip

BEAGLE also fills in missing genotypes. To use the imputed dosages for localGEBV as well, use beagle_impute_geno(geno), or sum each individual's two chromosome columns in geno_phased.

docs.title: Ordering the Map File
docs.text:
Map files must be ordered by:

  1. Chromosome
  2. Position

Example:

# simulate unordered map
map2 <- map[sample(1:nrow(map), nrow(map)), ]

# reorder map
map2 <- order_map(map = map2)

# order the map used for the rest of the tutorial, and put the genotype files in the same order
map         <- order_map(map = map)
geno        <- order_geno(geno = geno, map = map)
geno_phased <- order_geno(geno = geno_phased, map = map)

The order_map() function:

  • checks some formatting
  • converts non-numeric chromosome labels (e.g., "1A", "chr2") to numbers (set verbose = TRUE to print the conversion)
  • ensures proper ordering
  • standardizes column names (assumes columns are in the right order)

The order_geno() function puts a genotype file in the same order as the map, matching markers by name, and drops (with a warning) any markers that are not in both. See Pairwise LD for more details.

docs.title: Native LD Computation
docs.text:
The package contains a native LD calculator written in C++.

ld_pairs <- pairwise_ld(
  genotype_matrix = geno,
  parallelize     = FALSE,
  window          = NULL,
  min_r2          = NULL,
  min_obs         = 2L
)

docs.title: Important Notes
docs.text:
• window limits LD to markers within that many positions of each other, which keeps the size of the LD table manageable on dense marker panels
  • min_r2 drops weak pairs from the table
  • parallelize = TRUE processes chromosomes in parallel and is worthwhile on larger datasets
  • See Pairwise LD for all parameters

docs.title: Important Notes
docs.text:
• PLINK 1.9 MUST be installed to use this function! HapSelect looks in ~/bin and the system PATH, or the location set with set_plink_path()
  • See the Installation Guide and Configuration for more details
  • LD can be calculated externally, but must be provided in the same format as utilised in this package (see format_plink_ld() in Pairwise LD)
ld_pairs <- plink_pairwise_ld_geno(geno = geno, ld_window = 999999, 
                                ld_window_kb = 1e6, ld_window_r2 = 0)

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Description geno Dosage genotype matrix (whole numbers only) ld_window Maximum number of SNP pairs ahead to compute LD ld_window_kb LD window size in kb ld_window_r2 Minimum r² for a pair to be reported extra_args Additional PLINK arguments

Tip

Another function, plink_pairwise_ld(), can also be used if the .bed, .bim, and .fam files are already created. The prefix = argument can be utilized to provide the prefix to each of the files (e.g., files must be: prefix.bed, prefix.bim, prefix.fam).

docs.title: Loading Example LD Data
docs.text:
ld_pairs <- HapSelect::ld_pairs

The LD dataframe must contain the following columns:

c("Chrom", "Locus1", "Locus2", "Name1", "Name2", "LD")

docs.title: Other Information
docs.text:
Pairs not present (i.e., missing) in the data frame object are allowed and are handled in the haploblocking function.

Columns:

  • Chrom: the chromosome each SNP pair belongs to (numeric).
  • Locus1: numerical integer for the first marker in the marker pair. This should correspond to the order of the marker in the ordered map file above.
  • Locus2: similar to Locus1, this is the numerical integer of the second marker in the marker pair.
  • Name1: Character name of the first marker in the pair as seen in the genotype, map, and marker effects file.
  • Name2: Similar to Name1, this corresponds to the name of the second marker in the pair as seen in the genotype, map, and marker effects file.
  • LD: The numerical LD value computed. This is typically an \(\text{r}^{2}\) value.

docs.title: Constructing Haploblocks
docs.text: HapSelect has three haploblocking strategies, each passed to def_blocks() as a strategy object. This tutorial uses LD-based blocking from here on - see Haplotype Blocks for diagrams and the full parameter documentation of each strategy.

docs.title: LD-Based Blocking
docs.text:
haploblocks <- def_blocks(
  map         = map,
  strategy    = ld_strategy(
    ld        = ld_pairs,
    method    = "flanking",
    threshold = 0.3,
    tolerance = 3,
    tol_reset = TRUE,
    start     = "beginning",
    parallel  = FALSE
  )
)

docs.title: method
docs.text:
Controls how LD is evaluated when extending blocks.

Options:

  • "flanking" → compares the LD of the adjacent marker only (i.e., compares current first/last marker in the block to the next marker)
  • "average" → compares average LD across block (i.e., averages the next marker's LD to all markers currently in the block)

docs.title: threshold
docs.text:
LD cutoff (r²) used to terminate blocks.

Typical values:

0.3 to 0.7
  • Higher values create smaller haploblocks (great for greater resolution in QTL discovery applications)
  • Lower values are less aggressive, but may extend blocks past biological or statistical inference. Lower values may more fully capture QTL effects if heavily dispersed
  • In diverse datasets, lower values are generally needed, but in breeding lines (crops), higher values are likely better
  • Users should experiment with different LD thresholds to find which meets their needs

docs.title: tolerance
docs.text:
Allows temporary LD drops within a block. This may be caused by reference alignment error, genotyping error, or other issues. This value should be specified as a positive integer.

Example:

tolerance = 2

allows two low-LD markers before terminating the block. If the third marker meets the threshold, the block will not be terminated and all three markers will be included in the block.

docs.title: tol_reset
docs.text: If TRUE, tolerance resets after successful marker addition (i.e., sets the counter back to 0). If FALSE, the counter keeps iterating even after a successful marker addition and will terminate upon exceeding the integer specified and not include the marker(s).

docs.title: start
docs.text:
Controls how blocks initiate.

Options:

  • "LD" → start from strongest LD pairs and build to the left and to the right. The tolerance is unique to each side.
  • "beginning" → sequential chromosome scan starting from the first marker and only extending "right" (i.e., to the next marker based on position).

docs.title: Window-Based Blocking
docs.text:
Cuts blocks from the map alone, with no LD calculation, either every window markers ("window_snp") or every window map units ("window_map").

#every 50 SNP
haploblocks_window <- def_blocks(
  map      = map,
  strategy = window_strategy(window = 50, method = "window_snp")
)

#every 1 Mb (physical map) - use cM for a genetic map
haploblocks_window <- def_blocks(
  map      = map,
  strategy = window_strategy(window = 1e6, method = "window_map")
)

docs.title: Graph-Based Blocking
docs.text:
Builds blocks from a local LD graph, computing the LD it needs directly from the genotypes, so geno MUST be provided.

haploblocks_graph <- def_blocks(
  map      = map,
  geno     = geno,
  strategy = graph_strategy(
    theta_core   = 0.80,
    theta_extend = 0.20,
    theta_bridge = 0.20,
    theta_refill = 0.80
  )
)

#how many markers were placed and dropped on each chromosome
attr(haploblocks_graph, "graph_diagnostics")

Warning

Unlike the other strategies, graph-based blocking can leave some markers out of every block. See Haplotype Blocks for details.

docs.title: Convert Haploblocks to a Dataframe
docs.text:
The former function returns a list object which may be useful in some applications. This function will turn it into a more easily digestible format and report some information.

haploblocks <- block_obj_to_df(haploblocks, map)

docs.title: Summarise Haploblocks
docs.text:
Reports various summary statistics about blocks including average number of SNP per block, average size per block (not including single marker blocks), proportion of blocks comprised of a single marker, etc.

block_summary(block_df = haploblocks)

#compare against the other strategies
block_summary(block_df = block_obj_to_df(haploblocks_window, map))
block_summary(block_df = block_obj_to_df(haploblocks_graph, map))

docs.title: Loading Example Phenotypes
docs.text:
BLUE <- HapSelect::BLUE

BLUE was already loaded at the start of this tutorial - it is repeated here for clarity.

The BLUE dataframe should contain:

Column Description Column 1 Individual IDs matching the genotype file Column 2 A singular adjusted phenotype / BLUE / de-regressed BLUP

docs.title: Important Note
docs.text: We do not currently support other effects in the model or multiple observations per individual. If more advanced modelling is needed, please utilise other software. See the Documentation Overview for more details and alternative R packages for independent modelling.

docs.title: Compute Marker Effects
docs.text:
marker_effects <- create_marker_effects_file(
  geno = geno,
  BLUE = BLUE,
  h2_method = "VanRaden",
  ploidy = 2L,
  mean_impute = TRUE
)

The variance components and prediction accuracy are printed. This prediction accuracy is measured on the individuals used to train the model, so it will be optimistic - use the cross validation functions below with a large enough dataset for a fair estimate.

docs.title: h2_method
docs.text:
Controls scaling of marker variance to approximate narrow-sense heritability (for a true estimate, use GBLUP with some variation of REML to estimate).

Options:

  • "VanRaden" (recommended)
  • "marker_num" (only generally used if the genotype matrix was scaled; not applicable 99% of the time)

docs.title: ploidy
docs.text:
Integer ploidy level.

Must be provided as an integer. Example:

2L

NOT:

2

docs.title: mean_impute
docs.text: If TRUE (default), missing genotypes are replaced with the marker mean before fitting. If FALSE, the genotype matrix must not contain any NA values. See Marker Effects for more details.

docs.title: N-fold Cross Validation
docs.text:
CV <- n_fold_cross_validation(
  geno = geno,
  BLUE = BLUE,
  nfold = 5L,
  h2_method = "VanRaden",
  ploidy = 2L,
  mean_impute = TRUE
)

This splits the data up into 5L groups in this example and utilises 4 for training and 1 for validation. Each group is utilised once for valdiation.

New Options: - nfold the number of groups to split the data into as an integer

Note: Small datasets will yield unruly results if the training set is too small!

docs.title: Random Train/Test Cross Validation
docs.text:
CV <- cross_validation(
  geno = geno,
  BLUE = BLUE,
  train_prop = 0.9,
  fold = 30L,
  h2_method = "VanRaden",
  ploidy = 2L,
  mean_impute = TRUE
)

New Options: - train_prop the proportion of data utilised to train (rounded up) with the rest utilised for validation - fold the number of times to randomly sample a training and validation set with replacement, as an integer (default 30L)

Tip

Cross validation splits the data randomly. Use set.seed() beforehand to make the results reproducible.

docs.title: Computing localGEBV/haplotype effects
docs.text:
#load example data (or use the marker effects estimated above)
marker_effects <- HapSelect::marker_effects

#localGEBV
haploblock_obj <- compute_local_GEBV(
  geno = geno,
  marker_effects = marker_effects,
  haploblocks_df = haploblocks,
  set_missing_NA = TRUE,
  mean_adjust = TRUE,
  parallel = TRUE         #uses up to the number of cores allowed by set_cpu_cores()
)

#haplotypes
haplotype_obj <- compute_haplotype_effects(
  geno = geno_phased,
  marker_effects = marker_effects,
  haploblocks_df = haploblocks,
  set_missing_NA = TRUE,
  mean_adjust = TRUE,
  parallel = TRUE
)

The localGEBV and haplotype effects are kept in separate objects (haploblock_obj and haplotype_obj) so both can be carried through the rest of the tutorial.

docs.title: set_missing_NA
docs.text:
If TRUE:

  • any haploblock with ≥1 missing genotype becomes NA

If FALSE:

  • localGEBV is computed using the non-missing markers. This is equivalent to setting the dosage equal to the mean (i.e., contribution of 0 to localGEBV)

Warning

For set_missing_NA = TRUE: In practice, while many markers may pass missigness filters within a block, sometimes a block will have the vast majority of individuals with >= 1 missing genotype calls. This can artificially raise the variance. A missingness filter or imputation is recommended to avoid this: see Data Import and Imputation for more details.

docs.title: mean_adjust
docs.text:
Centers markers internally.

This is usually required because marker effects are typically estimated from centered genotype matrices. Only set to FALSE if you are highly confident in what you are doing!

Recommended for 99% of cases, otherwise GEBV and localGEBV will be biased (will not affect the haploblock variance, but will affect parent selection optimization):

mean_adjust = TRUE

docs.title: Important Information
docs.text:
A good confirmation things are working properly is to reconstruct GEBV from Zu, where Z is the centered dosage marker matrix and u are the marker effects. The mean should be 0 (or very close to it) and reflect GBLUP GEBV if using rrBLUP, BayesC, or GBLUP back solve methods. If the reconstructed GEBV mean is meaningfully away from 0, it indicates the wrong marker matrix (i.e., needs to be centered) is being used or the marker matrix was not centered when estimating marker effects.

The package will internally center markers if mean_adjust = TRUE. If the matrix is already centered, centering won't change the values or centering can be set to FALSE.

If you want genotype/haplotype configurations in the output to match the 0/1/2/# dosage format, provide the uncentered genotype matrix and set mean_adjust = TRUE. Otherwise, the reported genotype/haplotype configurations will reflect centered values. For clarity, you must provide dosage format (usually 0/1/2 for diploid, any integer for polypoid).

docs.title: Important Information
docs.text:
All visualisations are ggplot objects and can be modified accordingly like any other ggplot object. E.g., if one wishes to change the x-axis label of the Haploblock Positions Plot to "cM", the corresponding code would be:

haploblock_plot <- haploblock_plot + labs(x = "cM")

In the case of positions, the following can be used to convert the positions to Mb:

haploblock_plot <- haploblock_plot + scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(start, end, by), labels = as.character(seq(start, end, by) / 1e6), limits = c(start, end)) + labs(x = "Position (Mb)")
  • start and end represent the values (in base pairs/base units) to graph
  • by represents what to increment the axis labels by
  • Example: seq(0,1e9, 1e8) would create a vector with values every 100 Mb up to 1 Gb
  • breaks are where to create labels
  • labels specifies the labeling of the labels: seq(x,y,z) / 1e6 scales it to Mb and are then converted into characters
  • limits specifying the min and max values
  • labs(x = "Name") renames the x-axis

docs.title: Marker Effects Plot
docs.text:
marker_plot <- marker_effects_plot(
  marker_effects = marker_effects$Effect,
  chr = map$Chromosome,
  pos = map$Position,
  colors = c("#A01FF0", "#A7A8AA")
)

marker_plot
Parameter Description marker_effects Numeric vector of marker effects chr Numeric chromosome vector corresponding to each marker pos Numeric marker positions vector (genetic map or physical position) colors Vector of length 2 of alternating chromosome colors

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Chromosomes alternate between the two provided colors
  • Missing values (NA) are automatically removed before plotting
  • Chromosomes should generally be numeric for proper ordering

docs.title: Unique localGEBV/Haplotype Effects Plot
docs.text:
localGEBV_plot <- unique_localGEBV_effects_plot(
  haplo_obj = haploblock_obj,
  colors = c("#A01FF0", "#A7A8AA"),
  pos_type = "midpoint"
)

localGEBV_plot

haplo_eff_plot <- unique_haplo_effects_plot(
  haplo_obj = haplotype_obj,
  colors = c("#A01FF0", "#A7A8AA"),
  pos_type = "midpoint"
)

haplo_eff_plot
Parameter Description haplo_obj Object returned from compute_local_GEBV() or compute_haplotype_effects() colors Alternating chromosome colors pos_type "midpoint" or "start" positioning of haploblocks

docs.title: pos_type
docs.text: Option Description "midpoint" Plot effects at the midpoint of the haploblock "start" Plot effects at the first marker in the haploblock

docs.title: Funnel Plot
docs.text:
funnel_plot <- local_gebv_block_var_funnel_plot(
  haplo_obj = haploblock_obj,
  mean_line = FALSE,
  scale_colors = c("blue", "purple", "red")
)

funnel_plot <- haplo_block_var_funnel_plot(
  haplo_obj = haplotype_obj,
  mean_line = FALSE,
  scale_colors = c("blue", "purple", "red")
)

funnel_plot
Parameter Description haplo_obj Object returned from compute_local_GEBV() or compute_haplotype_effects() mean_line Adds dashed mean variance line scale_colors Vector of length 3 defining low/mid/high effect colors

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Haploblock variance is log-scaled and normalized between 0 and 1 for display
  • Useful for identifying high-effect haplotypes with large variance

docs.title: Haploblock Position Plot
docs.text:
haploblock_plot <- plot_haploblocks(
  haploblock_df = haploblock_obj$Haploblocks, #the original df can also be used here, `haploblock_df = haploblocks`
  block_fill = "#A01FF0",
  chrom_fill = NA,
  height = 0.30,
  single_width_bp = NULL
)

haploblock_plot
Parameter Description haploblock_df Haploblock dataframe block_fill Color of haploblocks chrom_fill Chromosome background color height Chromosome thickness single_width_bp Width of single-marker blocks (mostly deprecated)

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• chrom_fill = NA produces transparent chromosomes
  • Smaller height values create thinner chromosomes
  • Larger values create thicker chromosome tracks
  • single_width_bp does not control width of single marker blocks anymore: it is a mostly deprecated option

docs.title: Marker Density Plot
docs.text:
marker_density_plot <- plot_marker_density(
  map = map,
  bin_size = 500e3, #500 kb
  height = 0.3,
  chrom_fill = NA,
  col_low = "white",
  col_mid = "purple",
  col_high = "red"
)

marker_density_plot
Parameter Description map Ordered map dataframe bin_size Window size (based on position) used to count markers height Chromosome thickness chrom_fill Chromosome background color col_low Low-density color col_mid Mid-density color col_high High-density color

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Smaller bin_size values increase resolution but also increases noise
  • Larger bins produce smoother chromosome-wide density patterns. Really large values create awkward striping.
  • "Goldilocks principle" to select bin size - experiment a bit
  • Final bins are automatically capped at chromosome ends

docs.title: LD Decay Plot
docs.text:
ld_decay_plot <- plot_ld_decay(
  map = map,
  ld = ld_pairs,
  max_kb = 500,
  span = 0.3,
  k = 10L,
  method = "gam_cr",
  point_color = "#A7A8AA",
  curve_color = "#A01FF0",
  alpha = 0.2
)

ld_decay_plot
Parameter Description map Ordered map dataframe ld LD dataframe max_kb Maximum pairwise distance in kb to consider method Curve fitting method span LOESS smoothing parameter between 0 and 1 k Integer number of GAM basis functions point_color LD point color curve_color Fitted curve color alpha Point transparency between 0 and 1

docs.title: method
docs.text: Option Description "gam_tp" Thin-plate regression spline GAM "gam_cr" Cubic regression spline GAM "exp" Exponential decay model "loess" LOESS smoothing

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• "exp" guarantees monotonic decay and does not utilise k or span
  • span is only utilised by the loess method
  • Smaller span values follow local structure more closely, but may over fit
  • Larger span values produce smoother curves, but may over smooth
  • k is only utilised by the gam_cr and gam_tp methods
  • Lower k values smooth GAM curves more aggressively whereas higher values may overfit
  • "exp" will be quickest, but may miss local patterns and "gam_tp" is a good intermediate between speed and fitting local patterns

docs.title: Block Variance Manhattan Plot
docs.text:
variance_plot = block_variance_manhattan_plot(
  haplo_obj = haploblock_obj,
  colors = c("#A01FF0", "#A7A8AA"),
  pos_type = "midpoint"
)
variance_plot
Parameter Description haplo_obj haploblock object from compute_local_GEBV() or compute_haplotype_effects() colors defaults are c("#A01FF0", "#A7A8AA") and control the alternating chromosome colors pos_type either "midpoint" or "start" - controls where the block is plotted. The midpoint is the center of the block whereas the start is the first SNP in the block. For singleton blocks, it is the same.

docs.title: Haploblock Variance Plot
docs.text:
The haploblock position plot with each block coloured by its variance, showing where the high-variance regions sit on each chromosome and the block size.

block_var_plot <- plot_haploblocks_variance(
  haploblock_obj       = haploblock_obj,
  variance             = "Block_Var",
  scale_viridis_option = "magma",
  chrom_fill           = NA,
  height               = 0.30,
  single_width_bp      = NULL
)

block_var_plot
Parameter Description haploblock_obj haploblock object from compute_local_GEBV() or compute_haplotype_effects() variance Variance column to colour by, "Block_Var" or "Unique_Haplo_Block_Var" scale_viridis_option Viridis colour palette (e.g., "magma", "viridis", "turbo") chrom_fill Chromosome background color height Chromosome thickness single_width_bp Width of single-marker blocks

See Visualisations for more details.

docs.title: Selecting Haploblocks for the GA
docs.text:
Before running the genetic algorithm (GA), haploblocks can be filtered to reduce dimensionality and focus on the most important genomic regions. This will aid in convergence and computational efficiency. Generally speaking, as little as 10% of blocks may explain 90% of the genetic variance.

The select_top_blocks() function supports three different selection strategies.

docs.title: 1. Select the Top n Haploblocks
docs.text:
Selects the highest variance haploblocks directly.

haploblock_obj <- select_top_blocks(
  haploblock_obj = haploblock_obj,
  n = 15
)

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Description n Integer number of top haploblocks to retain based on block variance

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Very interpretable and simple.
  • Useful when a fixed number of blocks is desired.

docs.title: 2. Select the Top Percentage of Haploblocks
docs.text:
Selects the top proportion of haploblocks ranked by variance.

haploblock_obj <- select_top_blocks(
  haploblock_obj = haploblock_obj,
  perc_total = 0.5
)

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Description perc_total Proportion of haploblocks to retain (between 0 and 1)

Example:

perc_total = 0.5

Retains the top 50% of haploblocks ranked by variance (rounded up).

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Scales automatically with dataset size.
  • Less arbitrary than selecting a fixed number of blocks.
  • Still ignores cumulative variance explained.
  • May retain many low-information blocks in large datasets.

docs.title: 3. Select Haploblocks Explaining a Percentage of Total Variance
docs.text:
Retains the minimum number of haploblocks required to explain a specified proportion of the total haploblock variance.

haploblock_obj <- select_top_blocks(
  haploblock_obj = haploblock_obj,
  perc_of_total_var = 0.9
)

#the same selection for the haplotype effects object
haplotype_obj <- select_top_blocks(
  haploblock_obj = haplotype_obj,
  perc_of_total_var = 0.9
)

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Description perc_of_total_var Minimum proportion of cumulative block variance to explain between 0 and 1 (0 means none, 1 means all)

Example:

perc_of_total_var = 0.9

Retains enough haploblocks to explain at least 90% of the total block variance.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Usually the most biologically meaningful approach.
  • Dynamically adapts to the architecture of the trait.
  • Retains more blocks for highly polygenic traits.
  • Retains fewer blocks when major-effect haploblocks dominate.

docs.title: Comparison of Selection Strategies
docs.text:
Method Strengths Weaknesses Top n blocks Simple and interpretable Arbitrary cutoff Top percentage Scales with dataset size May retain weak blocks Variance explained Biologically adaptive Number of retained blocks varies between traits

To select all haploblocks, set n = nrow(haploblock_obj$Haploblocks), perc_total = 1, or perc_of_total_var = 1. This may seem redundant but is still needed for the GA.

docs.title: Computational Considerations
docs.text:
Increasing the number of retained haploblocks:

  • increases optimisation dimensionality
  • increases GA runtime
  • increases memory usage
  • may slow convergence substantially

However, retaining too few blocks may:

  • miss favourable rare haplotypes
  • oversimplify trait architecture
  • reduce long-term genetic gain potential

Users are encouraged to experiment with multiple selection thresholds depending on breeding goals and computational resources.

docs.text:
localGEBV_parent_obj <- local_gebv_parent_selection(
  haploblock_obj = haploblock_obj,
  n_founders = 20,
  popSize = 10,
  maxiter = 300,
  run = 150,
  strategy = "no_selfing",
  pmutation = 0.6,
  pcrossover = 0.6,
  maximize = TRUE,
  monitor = TRUE
)

haplotype_parent_obj <- haplotype_parent_selection(
  haploblock_obj = haplotype_obj,
  n_founders = 20,
  popSize = 10,
  maxiter = 300,
  run = 150,
  strategy = "OHS",
  pmutation = 0.6,
  pcrossover = 0.6,
  maximize = TRUE,
  monitor = TRUE
)

docs.title: GA Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Description haploblock_obj haploblock object from computing localGEBV/haplotype effects n_founders Integer number of founder parents to choose popSize Integer number of parental sets per simulation iteration maxiter Maximum iterations before termination run Iterations without improvement before termination strategy (localGEBV) Specify selfing to allow selfing (i.e., for the fitness function allow the same parent at a given block). If no_selfing requires two different parents per chosen block strategy (haplotype) OHS constrains the function to choose haplotypes from two different parents (can be identical, but must come from two individuals, most restrictive), OPV allows the same haplotype from the same individual to be utilised (least restrictive), Haploid_OHS is a hybrid approach where two different haplotyeps must be chosen, but it can be from the same parent. pmutation Mutation probability - swaps out one random individual for another from the total population pcrossover Crossover probability - swaps half of each population; if there is overlap, non-overlapping parents are chosen randomly from the total population maximize If TRUE, greater ultimate GEBV are better. If FALSE, lower ultimate GEBV are considered better monitor If TRUE, report the best and mean fitness each iteration (beside the progress bar, or printed when progress bars are off). If FALSE, no fitness information is reported.

Warning

If strategy is not specified, the least constrained strategy is used: "selfing" for localGEBV and "OPV" for haplotypes. Specify it explicitly, as above, for a realistic crossing scheme. See Parent Selection for all defaults.

The genetic algorithm (GA) balances:

  1. Exploration Searching broadly across possible parental combinations

  2. Exploitation Refining highly fit parental combinations already discovered

Improper parameter tuning can lead to:

  • premature convergence
  • failure to converge
  • excessive runtime
  • oscillation around suboptimal solutions

docs.title: popSize
docs.text: Controls the number of candidate parental sets evaluated per iteration.

docs.title: Trade-offs
docs.text:
Smaller popSize Larger popSize Faster individual iterations Slower individual iterations Less memory usage Higher memory usage Late convergence Better exploration and earlier convergence Higher risk of local optima Lower risk of local optima

Increasing popSize generally reduces the number of iterations needed for convergence, but each iteration becomes more computationally expensive.

docs.title: maxiter
docs.text: Maximum number of iterations allowed. Generally speaking, the greater the total population size available, the more iterations that are needed.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Too small → GA may terminate before convergence
  • Too large → unnecessary runtime after convergence

Generally:

  • small problems converge quickly
  • highly polygenic architectures with many parents/large populations may require many iterations
  • You will likely need to experiment

docs.title: run
docs.text: Number of iterations allowed without improvement before termination. Generally, I would not set this lover than 150 to 200, especially with low pmutation and pcrossover because exploring the parameter space may take awhile once close to being optimised.

docs.title: Trade-offs
docs.text: Smaller run Larger run Faster termination More exhaustive search May stop too early Longer runtime Risk missing optimum Better convergence stability

docs.title: pmutation
docs.text:
Mutation probability.

Mutation randomly substitutes one individual within populations from the total population.

docs.title: Trade-off
docs.text: Low mutation High mutation Stable convergence More exploration Risk local optima Risk instability and "overshooting"

docs.title: Important Notes
docs.text: Overly large mutation probabilities can prevent convergence entirely because high-performing parental sets are continuously disrupted. However, in practice, values of around 0.5 to 0.7 seem to be okay.

docs.title: pcrossover
docs.text: Probability populations exchange parental subsets (half of each pair swapped). If there are overlapping individuals after swapping, then the duplicates are dropped and non-duplicate individuals are randomly sampled from the total population.

docs.title: Trade-offs
docs.text:
Low crossover High crossover Less swapping Greater swapping Slower exploration Faster exploration More stable solutions Greater instability

Very high crossover rates may cause the GA to overshoot promising solutions and continuously disrupt near-optimal parental combinations. In practice, values of 0.5 to 0.7 seem to be okay.

docs.title: If convergence is unstable (i.e., asymptoptes and the mean goes down and up):
docs.text:
• decrease pmutation
  • decrease pcrossover
  • increase run

docs.title: If convergence is too slow:
docs.text:
• increase popSize
  • increase pmutation
  • increase pcrossover

docs.title: If solutions appear trapped in local optima:
docs.text:
• increase popSize
  • increase pmutation
  • increase pcrossover
  • increase run

docs.text: Parameter Description GA_output Output object from the GA geno and geno_phased Dosage (localGEBV) or phased (haplotype) genotype dataframe from before marker_effects Marker effects dataframe used previously map Ordered map dataframe used previously genetic_map_position Optional genetic map positions vector in centiMorgans in the same order as the map num_gen Integer number of recurrent truncation selection generations num_sim_reps Integer number of independent simulation replicates num_cross_per_gen Integer number of progeny generated per generation via random mating num_TS_parents Number of truncation-selected parents. If NULL, same as number of GA parents mean_adjust Whether to internally center genotypes (almost always TRUE) max_cM_chr Assumed chromosome genetic map length if no genetic map provided PCA Whether to compute PCA visualisation (TRUE or FALSE) colors Colors for PCA categories and simulation plot, must provide 4 alpha Transparency levels for PCA categories, must provide 4

docs.title: num_gen
docs.text: Controls how many generations of recurrent selection are simulated.

docs.title: Larger Values
docs.text:
• better evaluation of long-term gain
  • reveals genetic plateaus
  • better assesses diversity preservation

docs.title: Smaller Values
docs.text:
• faster simulation
  • focuses on short-term gain

docs.title: num_sim_reps
docs.text:
Controls the number of replicate simulations.

Replicates differ because of:

  • recombination randomness
  • parental chromosome sampling (Mendelian Sampling)

docs.title: Larger Values
docs.text:
Advantages:

  • smoother estimates
  • more reliable confidence intervals

Disadvantages:

  • increased runtime and memory

docs.title: num_cross_per_gen
docs.text: Number of progeny generated each generation.

docs.title: Larger Values
docs.text:
Advantages:

  • stronger selection intensity
  • improved ability to identify elite progeny
  • smoother trajectories
  • fewer instabilities from sampling effects

Disadvantages:

  • slower simulations
  • increased memory usage

docs.title: genetic_map_position
docs.text:
Optional vector of marker positions in centiMorgans (cM).

If omitted:

  • chromosomes are assumed to span max_cM_chr
  • genetic map positions are inferred proportionally from physical distance
  • The first marker on a chromosome would be 0 cM and the last would be 100 cM. A marker halfway in between (base pair position) would be 50 cM.

Providing a true genetic map is recommended whenever available.

docs.title: PCA
docs.text:
If TRUE, performs PCA on the genotype matrix and highlights:

  • GA-selected parents
  • TS-selected parents
  • overlapping parents
  • non-selected individuals

This helps visualise:

  • diversity retention
  • population structure
  • overlap between strategies

docs.title: HapSelect Workflow with Minimal Comments
docs.text:
Minimal workflow demonstrating:

  1. (Optional) VCF import, imputation, and phasing
  2. LD calculation
  3. Haploblock construction (LD, window, or graph)
  4. Marker effect estimation
  5. localGEBV/haplotype effect computation
  6. Visualisation
  7. GA parent selection
  8. Recurrent truncation selection simulation on GA selected parents and TS selected parents
