docs.title: Haplotype Blocks
docs.text:
Haplotype blocks (haploblocks) are contiguous genomic regions that are treated as a single unit for localGEBV, haplotype effects, and parent selection. HapSelect offers three ways to define them:

Strategy Groups markers by Needs Best suited to ld_strategy() Linear extension from the highest LD pairs Pairwise LD table The classic localGEBV haploblocking approach window_strategy() A fixed number of markers or a fixed map distance Map only Quick, LD-free blocking or a baseline comparison graph_strategy() Connected groups of markers in a local LD graph Genotype matrix Larger, more complete blocks with fewer singletons

docs.title: def_blocks()
docs.text:
All three strategies run through def_blocks(). A strategy holds how to block, while def_blocks() is given what to block.

haploblocks <- def_blocks(
  map      = map,                       #ordered map from order_map()
  strategy = ld_strategy(ld = ld_pairs), #ld_strategy(), window_strategy(), or graph_strategy()
  geno     = NULL                       #genotype matrix - required by graph_strategy() only
)

#turn the list object into a data frame for downstream steps
haploblocks <- block_obj_to_df(haploblocks, map = map)
Parameter Description strategy A strategy object built by ld_strategy(), window_strategy(), or graph_strategy() map Ordered marker map from order_map() geno Dosage genotype matrix. Required by graph_strategy(), which computes LD directly from it, and ignored (with a warning) by the other strategies

Warning

def_blocks() changed in v2.0.0. The LD parameters (ld, method, threshold, etc.) are no longer passed to def_blocks() directly - they now go into ld_strategy(). Code written for v1 will need to be updated!

docs.title: ld_strategy()
docs.text:
Grows blocks outward from seed marker pairs one marker at a time while LD stays high, using a pre-computed pairwise LD table (see Pairwise LD).

haploblocks <- def_blocks(
  map         = map,
  strategy    = ld_strategy(
    ld        = ld_pairs,
    method    = "flanking",
    threshold = 0.7,
    tolerance = 1,
    tol_reset = TRUE,
    start     = "LD",
    parallel  = FALSE
  )
)
Parameter Default Description ld Pairwise LD output from pairwise_ld(), plink_pairwise_ld(), or plink_pairwise_ld_geno() method "flanking" Block definition method ("flanking" or "average") threshold 0.7 Minimum r² value to consider adding a marker to the block (between 0 and 1) tolerance 1 Number of markers allowed to fall below threshold before terminating a block tol_reset TRUE If TRUE, reset the tolerance counter when a marker is successfully added to a block start "LD" Seed strategy for block boundaries ("LD" or "beginning") parallel FALSE Process chromosomes in parallel, using up to the number of cores allowed by set_cpu_cores() (see Configuration)

method

  • "flanking" → compares the LD of the adjacent marker only (i.e., compares current first/last marker in the block to the next marker)
  • "average" → compares average LD across block (i.e., averages the next marker's LD to all markers currently in the block)

tolerance

  • If the next marker to compare does not meet or exceed threshold, the counter is incremented by 1. Once the counter is greater than the tolerance value the block is terminated. Any markers between a successfully added marker and the block that did not meet the threshold will also be added to the block. This parameter helps to accommodate for reference alignment error, genotyping error, structural variation, and other systematic errors

tol_reset

  • TRUE the tolerance counter is reset to 0 when a marker meets the threshold.
  • FALSE the counter is not reset and will keep incrementing even if a marker is successfully added.

start

  • "LD" -> starts from the highest LD pair and the block will be extended both to the left and to the right according to the distance coordinate. The tolerance counter is reset between left extension and right extension.
  • "beginning" -> starts at the beginning of the chromosome, so blocks are only extended to the right.

Tip

threshold must be between 0 and 1 and tolerance must be a non-negative number, otherwise ld_strategy() will stop with an error before any blocking is attempted.

docs.title: How LD blocks are built
docs.text:
ld_strategy() walks along a chromosome and extends a block one marker at a time, absorbing markers while LD stays high and closing the block off to start a new one where it drops away. The diagrams below illustrate how the parameters above shape that process.

In each diagram, circles are markers laid out in physical order along the chromosome. A grey line is a strong link (LD ≥ threshold) and a dashed red line is a weak link (LD below threshold). A bracket underneath groups the markers that end up in one block, and an upright dashed red line marks a block boundary.

LD values in these diagrams are illustrative, chosen to make each behaviour visible.

LD blocking on 150 markers of the bundled example data (threshold = 0.7, start = "LD"). The triangle is the pairwise LD between markers; blocks form along the bottom from the highest LD pair down, not from left to right.

docs.title: Growing a block
docs.text:
A block grows outward from a seed. Each new marker (the candidate) is compared against the block; if the LD clears threshold the candidate joins. A marker that falls short isn't dropped straight away. It can be tolerated and absorbed if a later marker reaches back across it. Where LD stays too low, the block is closed off and the next block begins.

Here S2 is a weak link (0.61), but the block reaches across it to S3 (0.74 ≥ 0.70), so S2 is pulled in. Extension later runs out of road, so the block ends and S4 and S5 are left as their own single-marker blocks.

docs.title: method: what a candidate is compared against
docs.text: flanking compares the candidate to the block edge only; average compares it to the mean LD across the whole block. Same markers, opposite result: under flanking the weak LD(S3, S4) = 0.55 ends the block, while under average the strong ties to S1 and S2 lift the mean to 0.71 and S4 joins.

docs.title: tolerance: how many weak links a block bridges
docs.text: tolerance is the number of consecutive weak links the block may span before it gives up. On the same LD landscape, raising it bridges wider gaps, producing fewer, longer blocks and fewer singletons.

docs.title: tol_reset: whether an accepted marker forgives past misses
docs.text: Each weak link the block spans adds to a miss counter, and the block is closed off once that counter passes tolerance. tol_reset decides whether accepting a marker resets the counter. With tolerance = 2 in both rows below: under TRUE, absorbing S4 resets the counter, so the later weak link is affordable and the block runs to the end; under FALSE, the two early misses have already spent the budget, so the next weak link closes the block.

docs.title: start: where a block is seeded and which way it grows
docs.text: start sets the seed and the growth direction. "LD" seeds from the highest-LD adjacent pair and extends in both directions, resetting the tolerance counter between the left and right passes. "beginning" seeds at the first marker on the chromosome and extends rightward only.

docs.title: window_strategy()
docs.text:
Cuts blocks straight from the map with no reference to LD. Blocks are either a fixed number of markers or a fixed map distance. No LD table or genotype matrix is needed.

#fixed number of markers per block
haploblocks <- def_blocks(
  map         = map,
  strategy    = window_strategy(
    window    = 50,             #every 50 SNP
    method    = "window_snp"
  )
)

#fixed map distance per block
haploblocks <- def_blocks(
  map         = map,
  strategy    = window_strategy(
    window    = 1e6,            #1 Mb windows for a physical map (use cM for a genetic map)
    method    = "window_map"
  )
)
Parameter Default Description window Block size. A whole number of markers for "window_snp", or a distance in the map's own Position units (bp or cM) for "window_map" method "window_snp" "window_snp" (fixed number of markers) or "window_map" (fixed map distance)

method

  • "window_snp" → consecutive runs of window markers. The last block on a chromosome is short when the number of markers is not evenly divisible by window.
  • "window_map" → intervals of [0, window), [window, 2 × window), ... starting from position 0 on every chromosome. An interval with no markers produces no block, so the number of blocks follows marker density rather than chromosome length.

Warning

window is in the units of your map! For a physical map window = 1e6 is 1 Mb, but for a genetic map in cM it would be one block per chromosome. Fractional windows are allowed for "window_map", but "window_snp" requires a whole number.

Tip

Markers with a missing Chromosome or Position are dropped with a warning, and an unsorted map is sorted with a warning. Run order_map() first to avoid both.

docs.title: graph_strategy()
docs.text:
Graph-based blocking is a new implementation and is similar in concept to LD-based blocking. Rather than growing a block one marker at a time from a single chain of pairwise comparisons, it builds a sparse local LD graph over each chromosome and reads blocks off its structure, so a block is defined by how its markers hang together as a group. Because LD is only computed within a short window of each marker, it does not require genome-wide pairwise LD and LD is calculated internally from geno.

The method was developed by Jingyang Tong (QAAFI, The University of Queensland).

haploblocks <- def_blocks(
  map          = map,
  geno         = geno,              #required! LD is computed directly from the genotypes
  strategy     = graph_strategy(
    theta_core        = 0.80,
    theta_core_by_chr = NULL,
    theta_extend      = 0.20,
    theta_bridge      = 0.20,
    theta_refill      = 0.80,
    ld_min_r2         = 0.20,
    window_ld         = 20,
    window_core       = 20,
    window_extend     = 50,
    min_links         = 1,
    max_gap_snps      = 2,
    max_gap_markers   = 2,
    max_gap_position  = NULL,
    min_block_snps    = 2,
    parallel          = FALSE
  )
)

Warning

graph_strategy() MUST be given geno in def_blocks(), otherwise it will stop with an error. geno is aligned to map by marker name (see order_geno() in Pairwise LD), so markers missing from either file are dropped with a warning.

Graph blocking on one chromosome of the bundled example data with the default parameters: core edges, extension and bridge edges, the resulting components, linearisation (Stage II) and refill (Stage III). Each point is a marker, laid out by its LD connections rather than its map position.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Stage Description theta_core 0.80 I Minimum r² for a core edge between two markers theta_core_by_chr NULL I Named vector of per-chromosome theta_core overrides, e.g., c("1" = 0.9, "2" = 0.8) theta_extend 0.20 I Minimum r² for attaching an ungrouped marker to a block theta_bridge 0.20 I Minimum r² for a boundary edge that merges two adjacent blocks theta_refill 0.80 III Minimum r² for refilling a marker left inside a block's span ld_min_r2 0.20 I LD floor - edges below this are never stored window_ld 20 I Number of markers ahead of each marker to compute LD with window_core 20 I Maximum marker distance for a core edge window_extend 50 I Maximum marker distance to the nearest member of a block being extended min_links 1 I Minimum number of supporting edges for an extension max_gap_snps 2 I Maximum number of markers between two blocks that a bridge may cross max_gap_markers 2 II Maximum gap between consecutive members (in marker positions) before a block is split max_gap_position NULL II Maximum gap between consecutive members in map units before a block is split, or NULL for no limit min_block_snps 2 II Minimum number of markers for a segment to be kept parallel FALSE Process chromosomes in parallel, using up to the number of cores allowed by set_cpu_cores() (see Configuration)

All r² thresholds (theta_* and ld_min_r2) must be between 0 and 1, and all window, gap, and count parameters must be whole numbers. graph_strategy() will also stop with an error if ld_min_r2 is above theta_core, theta_extend, theta_bridge, or any theta_core_by_chr value, because edges below ld_min_r2 are never stored and those thresholds could never be applied. A window_core larger than window_ld produces a warning, since pairs beyond window_ld are never computed.

docs.title: How graph blocks are built
docs.text:
The method runs in three stages on each chromosome. In the diagrams below, circles are markers in physical order, arcs above the track are LD edges, and a bracket underneath groups the markers in one block. Light circles are markers that do not (yet) belong to a block.

LD values in these diagrams are illustrative, chosen to make each behaviour visible.

docs.title: Stage I: build blocks from a local LD graph
docs.text:
1. Core components - LD is computed between each marker and the next window_ld markers. Every pair with r² ≥ theta_core (and within window_core markers) becomes an edge, and each connected group of two or more markers becomes a core block. A core block does not have to be a contiguous run of markers: S6, S7, and S9 are connected without S8.
  2. Extension - each ungrouped marker joins a neighbouring block if it has at least min_links edges with r² ≥ theta_extend to that block and the nearest member of the block is within window_extend markers. If more than one block qualifies, the block with the most supporting edges is chosen, then the highest mean r², then the nearest. Markers are attached one at a time, so a marker that has just joined a block can pull in the next one.
  3. Bridging - adjacent blocks separated by no more than max_gap_snps markers are merged when any of the last three markers of one block has an edge with r² ≥ theta_bridge to any of the first three markers of the next. Bridging merges the two blocks, but it does not absorb the markers in the gap between them (S5 above).

Any marker still ungrouped at the end of Stage I becomes a one-marker block.

theta_core_by_chr

Some genomes have very different LD between chromosomes (e.g., the A, B, and D subgenomes of bread wheat), so a single theta_core may be too strict for some chromosomes and too lenient for others. theta_core_by_chr replaces theta_core for the chromosomes it names. Names must match the chromosome numbers in the map after order_map(), otherwise def_blocks() will stop with an error.

#a lower core threshold on chromosomes 1 and 2, theta_core everywhere else
strategy = graph_strategy(theta_core = 0.8, theta_core_by_chr = c("1" = 0.7, "2" = 0.7))

docs.title: Stage II: project blocks onto the map and keep segments that do not overlap
docs.text:
A block from Stage I is a set of connected markers, which can skip markers or jump across the chromosome. A haploblock must be a contiguous region, so each block is projected back onto the map:

  1. Split - members are put in map order, and the block is split wherever consecutive members are more than max_gap_markers positions apart (or more than max_gap_position apart in map units, if given). Segments with fewer than min_block_snps markers are discarded.
  2. Score - each candidate segment is scored as:
\[ \text{score} = 1000 \times n_{\text{markers}} + 100 \times \frac{n_{\text{markers}}}{\text{span}} - \log(1 + \text{length}) \]

where \(n_{\text{markers}}\) is the number of markers in the segment, span is the number of marker positions from its first to its last marker, and length is its map distance. The number of markers dominates, density breaks ties, and a shorter segment is preferred when both are equal.

  1. Select - segments are taken from the highest score down, and a segment is kept only if its whole interval is still free. A kept segment claims its entire interval, including any markers it skips, so this is a greedy selection rather than a search for the best overall set.

docs.title: Stage III: re-test the markers a selected block skipped
docs.text:
After selection, some markers sit inside a block's span without belonging to it. Each one is re-tested against the block that encloses it, and joins the block if its r² with any current member is ≥ theta_refill. LD is recomputed from the genotypes here, so window_ld and ld_min_r2 do not limit the comparison. Markers outside every selected block are kept as one-marker blocks.

Warning

A marker inside a block's span that fails the refill test is dropped and appears in no block. Unlike ld_strategy() and window_strategy(), the graph method does not guarantee every marker in the map is assigned to a block! On the bundled example data with the default parameters, 486 of the 6,070 markers are dropped. Dropped markers do not contribute to localGEBV or haplotype effects. Lowering theta_refill keeps more of them, and attr(haploblocks, "graph_diagnostics") reports how many were dropped on each chromosome (see below).

Warning

Do NOT estimate marker effects prior to using the graph approach! Marker effects should only be estimated with the final marker set!

docs.title: Diagnostics
docs.text:
def_blocks() attaches a per-chromosome summary to its output when using graph_strategy(). Inspect it before converting to a data frame, as block_obj_to_df() does not keep it:

haploblocks <- def_blocks(map = map, geno = geno, strategy = graph_strategy())

attr(haploblocks, "graph_diagnostics")
Column Description chromosome Chromosome number theta_core theta_core used on this chromosome, after any theta_core_by_chr override n_blocks Total number of blocks n_multi_marker_blocks Number of blocks with two or more markers n_single_marker_blocks Number of one-marker blocks n_markers_in Markers on the chromosome n_markers_out Markers placed in a block n_refilled Markers added back to a block in Stage III n_dropped Markers dropped in Stage III (in no block)

docs.title: block_obj_to_df()
docs.text:
Converts the block list object from def_blocks() to a data frame for downstream use. This is the same for every strategy.

haploblocks <- block_obj_to_df(haploblocks, map)

The resulting data frame has one row per haploblock:

Column Description Block Constituent markers, ; delimited Block_ID Unique block identifier, Chromosome:Block (e.g., "3:132" is the 132nd block on chromosome 3) Num_SNP Number of markers in the block First_SNP / Last_SNP First and last marker in the block Chrom Chromosome Start_Pos / End_Pos Map position of First_SNP and Last_SNP Block_Size End_Pos - Start_Pos (0 for single-marker blocks)

Warning

Do not use any kind of whitespace as a delimeter, this will not be considered a delimeter and will be part of the marker name!

docs.title: block_summary()
docs.text:
Reports basic statistics across all blocks.

block_summary(block_df = haploblocks)
Column Description Mean_SNP_per_Block / Max_SNP_per_Block Mean and maximum number of markers per block Mean_Block_Size / Max_Block_Size Mean and maximum Block_Size of multi-marker blocks Singleton_Blocks Number of single-marker blocks Percent_Singleton_Blocks Percentage of blocks that are single-marker blocks

Tip

Mean_Block_Size does not include singleton blocks (size 0) in the computation. It is the mean size of multi-SNP blocks. block_summary() is a quick way to compare strategies or parameter settings on the same data.

docs.title: Important Note
docs.text:
A custom haploblock dataframe may be provided for downstream steps. It must, however, be formatted the same with the same column names! At minimum, the Block, Block_ID, First_SNP, Last_SNP, and Chrom columns must be provided! The Block column should contain the list of markers in the block separated by ; (no whitespace!), the Block_ID should be a character and a unique identifier, First_SNP and Last_SNP should be the character name of the first and last SNP making up the block in Block, and Chrom should be a numeric positive integer value.

head(haploblocks)

docs.title: LocalGEBV
docs.text:
Local genomic estimated breeding values (localGEBV) quantify the breeding value contribution of each haploblock for each individual. The localGEBV are calculated as:

\[ \text{localGEBV}_{jk} = \sum_{i \in \text{block}_j} ({x_{ik}} - \overline{x_{i}}) \cdot \hat{\alpha}_i \]

where \(({x_{ik}} - \overline{x_{i}})\) is the centered (see VanRaden, 2008) allele dosage of individual \(k\) at marker \(i\) in haploblock \(j\), and \(\hat{\alpha}_i\) is the estimated marker effect. If mean_adjust = FALSE, then it is not centered and is the actual value.

This produces an \(\text{J × N}\) matrix of localGEBV values — one value per individual for \(N\) individuals per haploblock for \(J\) haploblocks — which captures the breeding value contribution of each genomic region separately.

Haploblock variance is then computed as:

\[ \text{var}(\mathbf{\text{localGEBV}_j}) = \frac{\sum_k \left( \text{localGEBV}_{jk} - \overline{\text{localGEBV}_j} \right)^2}{N} \]

docs.title: Haplotype Effects
docs.text:
Similarly, haplotype effects can be calculated as the per-chromosome contribution:

\[ \text{Haplotype}_{jkl} = \sum_{i \in \text{block}_j} ({x_{ikl}} - \frac{\overline{x_{i}}}{2}) \cdot \hat{\alpha}_i \]

where all terms are the same, except \(({x_{ikl}} - \frac{\overline{x_{i}}}{2})\) is the centered allele of individual \(k\) on chromosome \(l\) at marker \(i\) in haploblock \(j\) and the result is the haplotype effect of individual \(k\) for chromosome \(l\) and haploblock \(j\). The centered allele is equivalent to subtracting the allele frequency, p, from the allele in 0/1 format. Dividing the mean dosage by 2 is equivalent for a diploid where the mean is 2p. If the mean is equivalent to 2p for a diplid, then the mean of a haplotype (on average 1/2 of the GEBV) if simply p, which is the mean divided by 2.

This produces an \(\text{J × NL}\) matrix of haplotype effects — one value per individual per chromosome for \(L\) chromosome sets per haploblock for \(J\) haploblocks.

Variance is compute in the same fashion. However, because there are LN (LN = 2N for diploid) values per haploblock and each haplotype effect is less than a corresponding localGEBV (exactly 1/2 if the case of a completely inbred and homozygous population), the variance of haplotype effects is usually substantially less the variance of localGEBV. However, the ranking of blocks is still the same for completely inbred populations and likely highly correlated even for highly outbred populations. Thus, its intended purpose as a metric to choose informative haploblocks and assess genome architecture is nearly invariant to choose of localGEBV or haplotype effects.

docs.title: compute_local_GEBV() and compute_haplotype_effects() functions
docs.text:
#localGEBV
haploblock_obj <- compute_local_GEBV(
  geno           = geno,
  marker_effects = marker_effects,
  haploblocks_df = haploblocks,
  set_missing_NA = TRUE,            #if TRUE, any missing genotypes in a block will return NA for the localGEBV
  mean_adjust    = TRUE,            #centeres the genotype matrix - this should be TRUE in almost every case! Setting to FALSE will lead to biased localGEBV!
  parallel       = FALSE,           #if TRUE, process blocks in parallel
  chunk_size     = 100              #maximum number of blocks sent to a parallel worker at once
)

#haplotypes
haploblock_obj <- compute_haplotype_effects(
  geno           = geno_phased,
  marker_effects = marker_effects,
  haploblocks_df = haploblocks,
  set_missing_NA = TRUE,            #if TRUE, any missing alleles in a block will return NA for the haplotype effect
  mean_adjust    = TRUE,            #centeres the allele matrix - this should be TRUE in almost every case! Setting to FALSE will lead to biased haplotype effects!
  parallel       = FALSE,
  chunk_size     = 100
)
Parameter Default Description geno Dosage genotype matrix (compute_local_GEBV()) or phased genotype matrix (compute_haplotype_effects()). See Getting Started marker_effects Data frame with columns for SNP ID and estimated effect haploblocks_df Haploblock data frame from block_obj_to_df() set_missing_NA TRUE If TRUE, replaces localGEBV/haplotype effects for any individual with missing genotypes with NA mean_adjust TRUE Centers the genotypes, required in most cases parallel FALSE If TRUE, process haploblocks in parallel, using up to the number of cores allowed by set_cpu_cores() (see Configuration) chunk_size 100 Maximum number of haploblocks sent to a parallel worker at once. Only used when parallel = TRUE

Warning

Use the dosage genotype matrix (e.g., HapSelect::geno) with compute_local_GEBV() and the phased genotype matrix (e.g., HapSelect::geno_phased) with compute_haplotype_effects(). They are not interchangeable!

docs.title: set_missing_NA
docs.text:
-TRUE if a haplotype/marker configuration for an individual in a haploblock is missing \(>=\) 1 genotype call, the localGEBV value/haplotype effect for that individual's block is set to NA.

-FALSE localGEBV/haplotype effects are calculated with all non-missing genotypes. The missing genotypes are imputed to the mean. In the case of mean_adjust = TRUE, this is 0 and thus do not affect the value. For uncentered marker matrices, this is the genotype mean (\(2p\) for a diploid, or \(lp\) for other ploidy where \(l\) is ploidy and \(p\) is the alternative allele frequency). An individual missing every genotype in a block is still set to NA.

docs.title: mean_adjust
docs.text:
-TRUE centers the genotypes/alleles according to VanRaden, 2008. This is a necessary step in the vast majority of cases to prevent biasing localGEBV/haplotype effects and GEBV. It does not affect haploblock variance, but it may affect how parents are chosen in the GA.

-FALSE does not center the genotypes/alleles.

Warning

If marker effects are computed using an additive genetic model like GBLUP backsolve, rrBLUP, BayesC, etc., this WILL lead to biased localGEBV/haplotype effects and GEBV!!! Only set this to FALSE if you are confident in what you are doing!

docs.title: parallel and chunk_size
docs.text:
With parallel = TRUE, haploblocks are grouped into chunks of similar computational cost and the chunks are processed across parallel workers. Results are identical to parallel = FALSE.

  • Larger blocks (more markers or individuals) take longer, so chunks are balanced by estimated cost rather than by the number of blocks.
  • chunk_size caps the number of blocks in a chunk, which caps the amount of genotype data sent to each worker. Lower it if R runs out of memory in parallel mode.

Tip

Starting parallel workers takes a few seconds, so the benefit of parallel = TRUE grows with the number of blocks and individuals. On very small datasets it may not be faster than parallel = FALSE.

docs.title: Output Object
docs.text:
compute_local_GEBV() and compute_haplotype_effects() return a list with:

  • $Haploblocks — haploblock dataframe from Haplotype Blocks extended with:
    • Num_Uniq_Hap — number of unique haplotypes (marker or allele configurations for localGEBV and haplotype effects, respectively) observed in the block
    • Block_Var — population variance of localGEBV/haplotype effects across individuals (or chromosomes). This is the variance used to rank blocks
    • Unique_Haplo_Block_Var — population variance of the effects of the unique haplotypes, ignoring how often each occurs
  • $Haplotype_ID_Matrix - blocks (J) × individuals (K) or chromosomes (KL) matrix of unique localGEBV/haplotype IDs listed in $Haplotypes dataframe
  • $Haplotype_Effect_Matrix — blocks (J) × individuals (K) or chromosomes (KL) of haplotype effects/localGEBV values corresponding to $Haplotype_ID_Matrix IDs and $Haplotypes dataframe IDs and values.
  • $Haplotypes - dataframe containing the unique haplotype/genotype configurations in each haploblock as well as their localGEBV estimates, with columns:
    • Block_ID — the haploblock
    • Haplo_ID — unique ID of the haplotype, Block_ID:number (e.g., "1:2:3" is the 3rd unique haplotype in block 1:2)
    • Haplotype — the genotypes/alleles at each marker in the block, comma separated in marker order (e.g., "0,2,1")
    • Haplotype_Effect — localGEBV/haplotype effect of that configuration

docs.title: Marker Effects Input
docs.text:
The marker_effects data frame must have:

  • Column 1: SNP ID matching the map file
  • Column 2: Estimated marker effect (e.g., from rrBLUP::mixed.solve())

See Marker Effects for more information.

head(HapSelect::marker_effects)

docs.title: create_marker_effects_file()
docs.text:
This function was created to create the marker effects file using the geno input file and a new input called BLUE. It fits an rrBLUP model (via the rrBLUP R package) and returns the marker effects in the format required by the rest of the workflow.

marker_effects <- create_marker_effects_file(
  geno        = geno,
  BLUE        = BLUE,
  h2_method   = "VanRaden",
  ploidy      = 2L,
  mean_impute = TRUE
)
Parameter Default Description geno Dosage genotype matrix. See Getting Started BLUE Data frame of individuals and their BLUE/de-regressed BLUP/adjusted phenotype (see below) h2_method "VanRaden" Method used to scale the marker variance to approximate additive genetic variance ("VanRaden" or "marker_num") ploidy 2L Integer ploidy level mean_impute TRUE Replace missing genotypes with the marker mean before fitting

BLUE is a dataframe containing two columns:

  1. Individual, which gives the individual's identifier found in the genotype file, geno. Each individual MUST only appear once!
  2. BLUE, which contains a singular, numeric value. This value can be a Best Linear Unbiased Estimate (BLUE), de-regressed Best Linear Unbiased Prediction (BLUP) extracted from a random effect with an identity covariance structure (i.e., broad-sense heritability/repeatability effect with no additive genetic effect fit), or an adjusted phenotype.

Every individual in BLUE must be present in geno. Individuals in geno but not in BLUE are not used to fit the model. NA values in the BLUE column are allowed - those individuals are left out of the model fit and the prediction accuracy.

The function prints the estimated variance components and the prediction accuracy (the correlation between the GEBV and BLUE):

Marker Variance:           3.6773e-05
Additive Genetic Variance: 6.2044e-02
Residual Variance:         1.6562e-01
h2:                        0.27

Prediction Accuracy (cor(GEBV, BLUE or deregressed BLUP or adj pheno)) is: 0.78

Warning

The prediction accuracy printed by create_marker_effects_file() is calculated on the same individuals the model was trained on, so it will be optimistic. Use n_fold_cross_validation() or cross_validation() (below) to estimate how well the model predicts individuals it has not seen. However, prediction accuracy will be necessarily low with small datasets and using an n-fold subsampling or the bootstrap method with low training proportion.

docs.title: h2_method
docs.text:
Controls scaling of marker variance to approximate the additive genetic variance and thus narrow-sense heritability.

Warning

This is not a true additive genetic variance estimate. For a true value, it is better to use GBLUP with a REML variant to estimate the genetic variance.

docs.title: Options:
docs.text:
• "VanRaden" (recommended)
  • "marker_num" (only generally used if the genotype matrix was scaled; not applicable 99% of the time)

The "VanRaden" method is most commonly utilised in animal and plant breeding. It follows method 1 of Van Raden, 2008. The marker variance is multiplied by \(2*\sum{p_{i}(1-p_{i})}\) such that each marker is scaled equivalently and is assumed to contribute equivalent variance (infinitesimal model like GBLUP or BayesC). For other ploidy levels, the 2 is replaced with the ploidy.

"marker_num" should only be utilised when the genotypes have been pre-scaled to unit variance (i.e., not dosage values).

We plan to offer Yang's method in the future.

docs.title: ploidy
docs.text:
Integer ploidy level.

Must be provided as an integer. Example:

2L

NOT:

2

docs.title: mean_impute
docs.text:
• TRUE missing genotypes (NA) are replaced with the mean dosage of that marker before fitting the model and calculating prediction accuracy.
  • FALSE genotypes are used as provided. The model cannot be fit with missing genotypes, so this will fail with an error if geno contains any NA values.

Tip

Mean imputation is a simple approach that is reasonable for a small proportion of missing genotypes. For a large proportion, impute the genotypes first (e.g., with beagle_impute_geno(), see Data Import, Imputation, and Phasing).

docs.title: Resulting File Structure
docs.text:
Columns:

SNP Effect character value, marker names (must match geno and map) numeric allele substitution/marker effect value 
head(HapSelect::marker_effects)

This is the structure that must be provided if marker effects are provided externally.

Tip

We currently do not allow multiple marker effect columns at this time, but plan to add this functionality in the future as well as multi-trait capability.

docs.title: solve_marker_effects() and compute_prediction_accuracy()
docs.text:
create_marker_effects_file() is a wrapper around these two functions. They are exported for users who need the full model output, such as the variance components or intercept, rather than only the marker effects.

#fit the model - every argument must be given, there are no defaults
model <- solve_marker_effects(
  geno        = geno,
  BLUE        = BLUE,
  h2_method   = "VanRaden",
  ploidy      = 2L,
  mean_impute = TRUE
)

model$u   #marker effects
model$Vu  #marker variance
model$Ve  #residual variance

#correlation between the predicted GEBV and BLUE
accuracy <- compute_prediction_accuracy(
  geno           = geno,
  marker_effects = model,          #the model from solve_marker_effects(), not the marker effects data frame!
  BLUE           = BLUE,
  mean_impute    = TRUE
)

solve_marker_effects() returns the output of rrBLUP::mixed.solve(): a list with the marker effects (u), marker variance (Vu), residual variance (Ve), fixed effect (beta), and log-likelihood (LL). See the rrBLUP documentation for details.

compute_prediction_accuracy() returns the correlation as a 1 × 1 matrix. Use BLUE for a set of individuals not used to fit the model to estimate prediction accuracy on new individuals.

docs.title: Prediction Accuracy with Bootstrapping and Cross-Validation Methods
n_fold_cross_validation()
docs.text:
This function performs the marker effects calculation, but is utilised to evaluate model performance.

CV <- n_fold_cross_validation(
  geno        = geno,
  BLUE        = BLUE,
  nfold       = 5L,
  h2_method   = "VanRaden",
  ploidy      = 2L,
  mean_impute = TRUE
)

The data is split into nfold groups, where each group is utilised once for validation while training occurs on the other groups. That is, nfold - 1 groups are utilised for training and the remaining 1 group is utilised for validation. This is repeated until each group is utilised once for validation.

nfold MUST be an integer (i.e., 5L and not 5). The default is 5L.

The function prints the variance components for each fold and the mean prediction accuracy across folds, and returns the prediction accuracy of each fold.

docs.title: cross_validation()
docs.text:
CV <- cross_validation(
  geno        = geno,
  BLUE        = BLUE,
  train_prop  = 0.9,
  fold        = 30L,
  h2_method   = "VanRaden",
  ploidy      = 2L,
  mean_impute = TRUE
)

A more generalised version of n_fold_cross_validation(). This function splits the data into train_prop and 1 - train_prop proportions randomly each iteration. Across iteration, the sampling is conducted indepenently with replacement (i.e., bootstrapping). That is, similar groups could be utilised for training and validation in different iterations. Thus, more folds are likely needed compared to n_fold_cross_validation() to adequately assess uncertainty, but may be a better option for small datasets.

For small datasets, it is recommended that train_pop be closer to 1 or to make nfold a large integer, such that very few individuals are left out for training. This will, of course, necessitate more folds to assess accuracy.

train_prop must be a value between 0 and 1 (i.e., the proportion). The default is 0.9. This is taken as train_prop * number of rows rounded up. The rest of the data is utilised for validation.

fold is an integer value (e.g., 30L and not 30) that is utilised to repeat the random sampling with replacement fold times for fold validations. The default is 30L.

docs.title: Important Information
docs.text:
Warning

You should not try to utilise the validation functions on a small population size as it is highly inadvisable to train marker effects on small population sizes. What is considered "small" is relative to the number of markers, heritability, effective population size, and population structure. For crops, less than 200 individuals would be inadvisable. For livestock, this number is likely much greater. Both functions produce a warning when BLUE has 200 or fewer individuals.

Tip

Both cross-validation functions split the data randomly, so results will differ slightly between runs. Use set.seed() before calling them to make the results reproducible.

docs.title: Pairwise LD
docs.text:
Linkage disequilibrium (LD) between all marker pairs is the foundation of LD-based haploblock definition (ld_strategy(), see Haplotype Blocks). Before computing LD, the map and genotype files should be put into the same, sorted order. If your genotypes are in a VCF file, see Data Import, Imputation, and Phasing first.

Tip

window_strategy() does not use LD and graph_strategy() computes the LD it needs internally, so a pairwise LD table is only required for ld_strategy() and plot_ld_decay().

docs.title: order_map()
docs.text:
Sorts a marker map by chromosome and position. Required before LD computation and haploblocking.

map <- order_map(map = map, verbose = FALSE)
Parameter Default Description map Map file with the marker ID, chromosome, and position in the first three columns verbose FALSE If TRUE, print how chromosome labels were converted to numbers

The first three columns are renamed SNP, Chromosome, and Position. Markers with a missing chromosome are sorted last.

Non-numeric chromosomes

HapSelect requires numeric chromosomes. If the Chromosome column is not numeric (e.g., "1A", "chr2", "chrX"), every distinct label is sorted into natural order and numbered from 1. Natural order means "chr2" comes before "chr10":

map <- order_map(map = map, verbose = TRUE)
#> Chromosome labels were mapped to integers:
#>   chr2  -> 1
#>   chr10 -> 2
#>   chrX  -> 3

Warning

Labels that differ only in case or punctuation (e.g., "Chr1" and "chr1") are numbered as separate chromosomes, and labels that look like missing values (e.g., "NA", ".", "unknown") are numbered as real chromosomes. Both produce a warning - fix these labels yourself before ordering the map!

Non-character marker IDs and non-numeric positions are also coerced with a warning. Check the output is what you expect.

Tip

Run order_map() once and use the resulting map everywhere downstream. The chromosome numbers it assigns are what theta_core_by_chr in graph_strategy() and the plotting functions will refer to.

docs.title: order_geno()
docs.text:
Puts a genotype matrix into the same order as an ordered map and keeps only the markers in both. order_map() only reorders the three map columns, so use order_geno() to bring the genotypes along with it.

map  <- order_map(map = map)
geno <- order_geno(geno = geno, map = map)
Parameter Default Description geno Genotype matrix (dosage or phased), with the marker ID, chromosome, and position in the first three columns map NULL Ordered map from order_map(). If NULL, geno is ordered by its own first three columns instead verbose FALSE Passed to the chromosome numbering when map = NULL

Markers are matched by name, not by row, so geno can arrive in any order. The chromosome and position columns of the result are taken from map.

  • Markers in geno but not map, or in map but not geno, are dropped with a warning listing (up to five of) them.
  • Duplicated marker IDs in either file are an error, because a marker could not be matched to one row.
  • map must already have numeric chromosomes - run order_map() on it first.

Tip

Because only shared markers are kept, a smaller map can be used to extract a subset of markers from a large genotype matrix, e.g., order_geno(geno, map[map$Chromosome == 1, ]) for chromosome 1 only.

docs.title: pairwise_ld()
docs.text:
Computes pairwise r² values between markers within each chromosome using HapSelect's internal C++ implementation. Markers on different chromosomes are never compared.

ld_pairs <- pairwise_ld(
  genotype_matrix = geno,
  parallelize     = FALSE,
  window          = NULL,
  min_r2          = NULL,
  min_obs         = 2L
)
Parameter Default Description genotype_matrix Dosage genotype matrix. See HapSelect::geno for formatting examples or Getting Started parallelize FALSE Process chromosomes in parallel, using up to the number of cores allowed by set_cpu_cores() (see Configuration) window NULL Only compare markers at most this many positions apart. NULL compares every pair on a chromosome min_r2 NULL Drop pairs with r² below this value. NULL keeps every pair min_obs 2L Number of individuals that must be observed (non-missing) at both markers for an r² to be computed

window

Without a window, the number of pairs grows with the square of the number of markers on a chromosome, so dense panels produce very large tables. A window keeps the number of pairs proportional to the number of markers. Choose a window larger than the longest block you expect to find with ld_strategy(), as pairs outside the window are missing from the table and are handled as missing by the haploblocking function.

min_obs

Two individuals always lie on a straight line, so a pair observed in only two individuals gives r² = 1 whatever the genotypes were. Raising min_obs to 3L (or higher) refuses those pairs, at the cost of losing pairs between sparsely genotyped markers.

Tip

A pair whose r² is undefined (one marker is monomorphic, or fewer than min_obs individuals are observed at both markers) is left out of the table rather than returned as NA.

parallelize

Work is split by chromosome. If pairwise_ld() is run serially without a window on a dataset with more than ~1,000 markers on a chromosome, it will print a message suggesting parallelize = TRUE. Set parallelize = FALSE explicitly to silence it.

docs.title: plink_pairwise_ld_geno() and plink_pairwise_ld()
docs.text:
Wraps PLINK v1.9 for LD computation. This can be computed from geno or from a PLINK binary fileset (.bed/.bim/.fam).

#from scratch with a genotype file:
ld_pairs <- plink_pairwise_ld_geno(geno = geno, ld_window = 999999,
                                   ld_window_kb = 1e6, ld_window_r2 = 0)

#with the PLINK fileset already made:
ld_pairs <- plink_pairwise_ld("path/to/plink_prefix")

Warning

PLINK 1.9 MUST be installed in order to use these functions. If it cannot be found you will get an error message. See Installation for more details, or use set_plink_path() to point HapSelect at a specific executable (see Configuration).

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Description geno Genotype matrix used throughout HapSelect. See HapSelect::geno for formatting examples or Getting Started prefix PLINK binary prefix for .bed .bim and .fam files (e.g., prefix.bed) ld_window 999999 Maximum number of SNP pairs ahead to compute LD ld_window_kb 1000000 Maximum window size in kb to compute LD ld_window_r2 0 Minimum r² for a pair to be reported extra_args character() Additional PLINK arguments, e.g., c("--maf", "0.05")

Warning

PLINK reads hard genotype calls, so dosages in geno must be whole numbers (0/1/2). Fractional dosages (e.g., from read_vcf_geno(prefer_ds = TRUE)) cannot be written to PLINK format - use pairwise_ld() for those instead.

Tip

PLINK is limited to the number of cores allowed by set_cpu_cores(). To override this for a single call, pass --threads in extra_args, e.g., extra_args = c("--threads", "4").

docs.title: format_plink_ld()
docs.text:
If you would rather run PLINK yourself, format_plink_ld() converts a PLINK --r2 output file into the HapSelect LD format.

ld_pairs <- format_plink_ld(
  ld_path = "path/to/plink_output.ld",     #output of plink --r2
  bim     = "path/to/plink_prefix.bim"     #.bim file of the fileset LD was computed from
)

Locus1 and Locus2 are taken from the order of the markers in the .bim file, restarting at 1 on each chromosome, so the .bim file must be in the same order as the ordered map.

Warning

PLINK's own defaults (--ld-window 10 --ld-window-kb 1000 --ld-window-r2 0.2) are much stricter than HapSelect's, and only report pairs within 10 markers with r² ≥ 0.2. On chromosome 1 of the example data this returns 490 pairs instead of 45,451! To match plink_pairwise_ld(), run PLINK with --r2 --ld-window 999999 --ld-window-kb 1000000 --ld-window-r2 0.

docs.title: Loading Example LD Data
docs.text:
ld_pairs <- HapSelect::ld_pairs

The LD dataframe must contain the following columns:

c("Chrom", "Locus1", "Locus2", "Name1", "Name2", "LD")

docs.title: Other Information
docs.text:
Pairs not present (i.e., missing) in the data frame object are allowed and are handled in the haploblocking function.

Columns:

  • Chrom: the chromosome each SNP pair belongs to (numeric).
  • Locus1: numerical integer for the first marker in the marker pair. This should correspond to the order of the marker in the ordered map file above, counting from 1 on each chromosome.
  • Locus2: similar to Locus1, this is the numerical integer of the second marker in the marker pair.
  • Name1: Character name of the first marker in the pair as seen in the genotype, map, and marker effects file. Names must match exactly
  • Name2: Similar to Name1, this corresponds to the name of the second marker in the pair as seen in the genotype, map, and marker effects file.
  • LD: The numerical LD value computed. This is typically an \(\text{r}^{2}\) value, and must be between 0 and 1.
head(HapSelect::ld_pairs)

docs.title: How the Genetic Algorithm Works
docs.text:
The HapSelect genetic algorithm (GA) for localGEBV or haplotype effects attempts to identify a founder set of individuals from a larger population that maximises the potential to recover favourable localGEBV or haplotype effects across the selected haploblocks.

Rather than optimising overall GEBV directly, which often limits diversity, the GA optimises the ability of the selected founder pool to produce elite offspring across genomic regions if the best regions could be simultaneously combined. This is the core idea behind "The Ultimate Genotype" presented in Hayes et al., 2024. While it is currently impossible to construct an ultimate genotype in practice, these tools excel in maintaining diversity while providing potential for long-term genetic gain in breeding programs. The package implements fitness functions that the GA uses to optimise for both localGEBV and haplotype effects with different strategies (see package citation). Custom fitness functions can also be provided - we plan to offer an extensive guide to this in the future.

The GA core algorithm relies on the following R package while the fitness, mutation, and crossover functions are custom designed in HapSelect:

GA: Genetic Algorithms

docs.title: The Optimisation Objective
docs.text:
For each haploblock:

  1. All possible pairwise crosses among the selected founders (localGEBV) or chromosomes (haplotypes) are evaluated
  2. Combinations that violate optimisation conditions (for example, selfing in localGEBV or haplotypes derived from the same parent with optimal haplotype stacking) are removed. This depends on the strategy argument.
  3. The expected offspring localGEBV for each cross is calculated (average of parental localGEBV or sum of chosen haplotypes)
  4. The highest-scoring cross for that haploblock is retained
  5. The process repeats across all haploblocks
  6. The average localGEBV or haplotype sums ("fitness") values are summed across haploblocks to determine "The Ultimate GEBV" for each set of founders across the entire genome.

The GA therefore attempts to maximise:

  • favourable haplotype complementarity
  • genomic coverage of elite haplotypes
  • the best achievable offspring configuration across blocks that meet optimisation constraints (e.g., limited starting founders from a large population)

rather than simply selecting the individuals with the highest total GEBV (truncation selection, TS).

docs.title: localGEBV
docs.text:
Conceptually, the fitness function is:

$$ \mathrm{Fitness} = \sum_{j=1}^{J} \max_{(i,k)} \left( \frac{localGEBV_{ij} + localGEBV_{kj}}{2} \right) $$ where:

Symbol Meaning J Number of selected haploblocks \(localGEBV_{i/kj}\) localGEBV of individual i or k at haploblock j (i,k) Pairwise unique founder combinations (same for all haploblocks)

For each block, the GA identifies the founder pair with the highest expected offspring breeding value (EBV) and sums these optimal values across all blocks.

docs.title: Selfing vs no-selfing at a block
docs.text: At a single block the GA keeps the best cross among the selected founders, where a cross's progeny value is the mid-parent average of the two parents' localGEBV. With strategy = "no_selfing" the two parents must be distinct; with strategy = "selfing" a founder may be crossed with itself, which lets a block lock in its single best founder rather than averaging two individuals. Selfing therefore never lowers a block's value, but constrains diversity.

docs.title: True Haplotypes
docs.text:
The true haplotype fitness function is as follows:

$$ \mathrm{Fitness} = \sum_{j=1}^{J} \max_{(il,kl)}({haplotype_{ijl} + haplotype_{kjl}}) $$ where:

Symbol Meaning J Number of selected haploblocks \(haplotype_{i/kjl}\) haplotypes of individual i and k at haploblock j (il,kl) Pairwise unique haplotype combinations (same for all haploblocks)

docs.title: Haplotype Selection Strategies
docs.text:
The localGEBV fitness above scores each founder by its diploid value at a block. HapSelect can instead work at the haplotype level: each founder contributes its two phased chromosomes, and a genotype's value at a block is the sum of the two chosen haplotype effects. Three strategies control which haplotype pairings are allowed at each block:

Tip

The possible combinations of ijl and ikl depend on strategy. For example, strategy = "OHS" adds the constraint that \(i \neq k\), while \(l\) is free to be any chromosome within an individual. That is, haplotypes must come from different individuals. The strategy = "OPV" allows for \(i = k\) and \(l\) to be the same value (in other words, the same haplotype can be chosen twice). The strategy = "Haploid_OHS" allows \(i = k\), but \(l\) must be two different values - or in other words, the same individual can be used, but it must be different chromosomes.

  • OPV (Optimal Population Value) — any haplotype may be paired with itself, so a block's ceiling is its single best haplotype doubled. This represents a fully homozygous ideal line.
  • Haploid_OHS — the two haplotypes must be distinct, but may come from the same founder (for example an individual's two homologs), as achievable through doubled haploids.
  • OHS (Optimal Haplotype Selection) — the two haplotypes must come from different founders, representing a realistic biparental cross.

As with localGEBV, the per-block winners are summed into the genome-wide total. Because each strategy restricts the allowed pairings further, the ultimate GEBV always ranks OPV ≥ Haploid_OHS ≥ OHS.

Warning

Both localGEBV and haplotype methods only work for diploids currently. We plan to expand the localGEBV method to non-diploid soon.

docs.title: The genome-wide total
docs.text: The per-block winners are summed into the ultimate predicted-progeny GEBV. Because each block is optimised independently, different founder pairs can win different blocks. This is the complementarity the GA is built to exploit.

docs.title: Why This Differs From Truncation Selection
docs.text:
Traditional truncation selection (TS):

  • selects the individuals with the highest overall GEBV
  • tends to repeatedly favour the same highly elite individuals
    • these individuals are often related (clustered on the PCA) and therefore share similar "good" and "bad" genomic segments. This increases inbreeding more quickly as well as unfavourable LD.
  • may rapidly reduce diversity

In contrast, the HapSelect GA:

  • searches for complementary founder combinations
  • rewards founder sets that collectively cover favourable haplotypes/localGEBV
  • allows different founders to contribute to different genomic regions
  • can retain valuable rare haplotypes ignored by standard TS

This means an individual with only moderate total GEBV may still be highly valuable if it contributes an elite haplotype at a specific high-variance block.

docs.title: Pairwise Crossing Strategy
docs.text:
The GA assumes that:

  • favourable haplotypes can be combined through recombination
  • different founder pairs may be optimal for different haploblocks
  • no single founder pair is necessarily optimal genome-wide

For each haploblock, the algorithm evaluates:

combn(founders, 2)

to test all possible pairwise combinations among the selected founders. In the case of haplotypes, founders is actually haplotype pairs (e.g., for a diploid, 2 possible haplotypes per individual).

docs.title: Evolutionary Search Procedure
docs.text:
The GA evolves founder sets over multiple iterations using:

Operation Purpose Population initialisation Generate random founder sets Fitness evaluation Score founder sets using haploblock complementarity Mutation Randomly replace a single founder in each population Crossover Swap part of two founder sets

The search attempts to balance:

  • exploration of new founder combinations
  • exploitation of high-performing founder sets

docs.title: Mutation
docs.text:
Mutation randomly replaces one founder within a solution:

#expressed in probability: i.e., between 0 and 1
pmutation = 0.6 #default

Higher mutation rates:

  • increase exploration
  • reduce risk of local optima

but may:

  • destabilise convergence
  • slow optimisation if many "good" founder sets are systematically disrupted every generation

docs.title: Crossover
docs.text:
Crossover exchanges founders between two high-performing solutions.

The algorithm:

  1. Takes a random half of the founders from one solution
  2. Combines them with all of the founders in the other solution, dropping duplicates
  3. Randomly samples the combined set back down to n_founders (or, if there are too few founders after dropping duplicates, tops it up with random individuals from the total population)

Each crossover produces two new solutions, one starting from each parent solution.

This helps preserve useful founder combinations while still exploring new combinations.

docs.title: Interpretation of the Final Founder Set
docs.text:
The final GA-selected founder set should (generally) be interpreted as:

  • a complementary breeding population
  • a set of parents with strong collective haplotype coverage
  • a founder pool optimised for long-term recombination potential

rather than simply the top individuals ranked by overall GEBV.

docs.title: Preparing Input - select_top_blocks()
docs.text:
Select top haploblocks by Block_Var. The select_top_blocks() function can select blocks in three different ways and returns a modified haploblock_obj object by adding on two additional dataframes to the list structure.

#select the top n blocks using the n argument
haploblock_obj <- select_top_blocks(
  haploblock_obj = haploblock_obj,
  n = 15
)

#select the top x% of blocks using the perc_total argument
haploblock_obj <- select_top_blocks(
  haploblock_obj = haploblock_obj,
  perc_total = 0.5
)

#select the number of blocks explaining at least x% of the total block variance utilising the perc_of_total_var argument
haploblock_obj <- select_top_blocks(
  haploblock_obj = haploblock_obj,
  perc_of_total_var = 0.9
)
  • n = number requires an integer number of blocks, denoted by number to select with the greatest haploblock variance
  • perc_total denotes the proportion (between 0 and 1) of blocks to select (rounded up) from the total number of blocks with the greatest variance
  • perc_of_total_var denotes selecting the proportion (between 0 and 1) of blocks (rounded up) that explain at least that proportion of the total block variance and have the greatest variance (i.e., the minimum number of blocks required to achieve the target proportion). This is the recommended option to use because it:
    • Is usually the most biologically meaningful approach.
    • Dynamically adapts to the architecture of the trait.
    • Retains more blocks for highly polygenic traits.
    • Retains fewer blocks when major-effect haploblocks dominate.

docs.title: Comparison of Selection Strategies
docs.text:
Method Strengths Weaknesses Top n blocks Simple and interpretable Arbitrary cutoff Top percentage Scales with dataset size May retain weak blocks or discard high-variance blocks Variance explained Biologically adaptive Number of retained blocks varies between traits and architecture

The output is a modified haploblock_obj that contains subsetted matrices and dataframes needed for the GA:

  • $Haploblocks_GA — the selected rows of $Haploblocks, ordered from the highest to lowest Block_Var
  • $Haplotype_Effect_Matrix_GA — the localGEBV/haplotype effects of the selected blocks, with individuals (or chromosomes) as rows and blocks as columns

Only one of n, perc_total, or perc_of_total_var may be given. n cannot be larger than the number of blocks, and perc_total and perc_of_total_var must be between 0 and 1.

docs.title: Computational Considerations
docs.text:
Increasing the number of retained haploblocks:

  • increases optimisation dimensionality
  • increases GA runtime
  • increases memory usage
  • may slow convergence substantially

However, retaining too few blocks may:

  • miss favourable rare haplotypes
  • oversimplify trait architecture
  • reduce long-term genetic gain potential
  • may ignore how the contribution small, cumulative effects have to overall fitness and optimisation

Users are encouraged to experiment with multiple selection thresholds depending on breeding goals and computational resources. The Basic Simulation functions will be useful for interpreting the GA output.

docs.title: GA Functions
docs.text:
Warning

These individuals are selected via a heuristic search optimisation and are thus never guaranteed to be the best set of individuals! The heuristic search optimisation is necessary to make most problems computationally feasible. Generally, unless stuck in a very pre-mature local optima, the results are the best or close to the best solution. Furthermore, more than one unique set of parents with the same overall fitness may exist in smaller scenarios. The GA sub object contains all solutions.

localGEBV_parent_obj <- local_gebv_parent_selection(
  haploblock_obj = haploblock_obj,  #output of select_top_blocks() on compute_local_GEBV() output
  strategy       = "no_selfing",
  n_founders     = 20,
  popSize        = 100,
  maxiter        = 500,
  run            = 50,
  pmutation      = 0.6,
  pcrossover     = 0.6,
  maximize       = TRUE,
  monitor        = TRUE
)

haplotype_parent_obj <- haplotype_parent_selection(
  haploblock_obj = haploblock_obj,  #output of select_top_blocks() on compute_haplotype_effects() output
  strategy       = "OHS",
  n_founders     = 20,
  popSize        = 100,
  maxiter        = 500,
  run            = 50,
  pmutation      = 0.6,
  pcrossover     = 0.6,
  maximize       = TRUE,
  monitor        = TRUE
)

Warning

haploblock_obj MUST be the output of select_top_blocks(), otherwise the GA functions will stop with an error. To use every block, use select_top_blocks(haploblock_obj, perc_total = 1).

Parameter Default Description haploblock_obj Output of select_top_blocks() strategy "selfing" (localGEBV) / "OPV" (haplotypes) Whether to allow selfing (localGEBV) or constraints on haplotype pairing (haplotypes). See below n_founders 20 Integer number of parents to choose popSize 100 Integer number of parental sets per iteration maxiter 500 Maximum iterations before termination run 50 Iterations without improvement before terminating pmutation 0.6 Mutation probability — swaps out one random individual for another from the total population pcrossover 0.6 Crossover probability — combines two parental sets; if there is overlap, non-overlapping parents are chosen randomly from the total population maximize TRUE If TRUE, maximise the ultimate GEBV. If FALSE, minimise it monitor TRUE If TRUE, report the best and mean fitness each iteration

docs.title: strategy
docs.text:
Function Options Default local_gebv_parent_selection() "selfing", "no_selfing" "selfing" haplotype_parent_selection() "OPV", "Haploid_OHS", "OHS" "OPV"

See The Fitness Function above for what each option allows.

Warning

The defaults are the least constrained strategies, which give the highest ultimate GEBV but may not represent a realistic crossing scheme. For a biparental crossing program, specify strategy = "no_selfing" (localGEBV) or strategy = "OHS" (haplotypes) explicitly.

docs.title: monitor
docs.text:
• TRUE → while progress bars are shown, the best and mean fitness of the current iteration are displayed beside the parent selection bar. When progress bars are off (e.g., in a batch job), one line is printed per iteration instead:
Iter    1 | Best = 1.541 | Mean = 1.492 | SD = 0.028
Iter    2 | Best = 1.542 | Mean = 1.502 | SD = 0.026
  • FALSE → no fitness information is shown. The progress bar is still drawn.

See Progress Reporting for more information.

docs.title: maximize
docs.text:
The GA can only maximise, so minimisation is performed by multiplying the fitness by -1. The fitness values in the returned GA object are converted back to the original scale.

The genetic algorithm (GA) balances:

  1. Exploration Searching broadly across possible parental combinations

  2. Exploitation Refining highly fit parental combinations already discovered

Improper parameter tuning can lead to:

  • premature convergence
  • failure to converge
  • excessive runtime
  • oscillation around suboptimal solutions

docs.title: popSize
docs.text: Controls the number of candidate parental sets evaluated per iteration.

docs.title: Trade-offs
docs.text:
Smaller popSize Larger popSize Faster individual iterations Slower individual iterations Less memory usage Higher memory usage Late convergence Better exploration and earlier convergence Higher risk of local optima Lower risk of local optima

Increasing popSize generally reduces the number of iterations needed for convergence, but each iteration becomes more computationally expensive.

docs.title: maxiter
docs.text: Maximum number of iterations allowed.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Too small → GA may terminate before convergence
  • Too large → unnecessary runtime after convergence

Generally:

  • small problems converge quickly
  • highly polygenic architectures with many parents may require many iterations

docs.title: run
docs.text: Number of iterations allowed without improvement before stopping.

docs.title: Trade-offs
docs.text: Smaller run Larger run Faster termination More exhaustive search May stop too early Longer runtime Risk missing optimum Better convergence stability

docs.title: pmutation
docs.text:
Mutation probability.

Mutation randomly substitutes one individual within populations from the total population. Values between 0.5 and 0.75 seem to be fairly optimal so far.

docs.title: Trade-off
docs.text: Low mutation High mutation Stable convergence More exploration Risk local optima Risk instability and "overshooting"

docs.title: Important Notes
docs.text: Overly large mutation probabilities can prevent convergence entirely because high-performing parental sets are continuously disrupted.

docs.title: pcrossover
docs.text: Probability populations exchange parental subsets (half of each pair swapped). If there are overlapping individuals after swapping, then the duplicates are dropped and non-duplicate individuals are randomly sampled from the total population. Values between 0.50 and 0.75 seem to be optimal so far.

docs.title: Trade-offs
docs.text:
Low crossover High crossover Less swapping Greater swapping Slower exploration Faster exploration More stable solutions Greater instability

Very high crossover rates may cause the GA to overshoot promising solutions and continuously disrupt near-optimal parental combinations.

docs.title: If convergence is unstable:
docs.text:
• decrease pmutation
  • decrease pcrossover
  • increase run

docs.title: If convergence is too slow:
docs.text:
• increase popSize
  • increase pmutation
  • increase pcrossover

docs.title: If solutions appear trapped in local optima:
docs.text:
• increase popSize
  • increase pmutation
  • increase run

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
# One optimal set of selected parents
parent_obj$selected_founders

#GA information and statistics over iterations
parent_obj$GA

#plot the best, mean, and median fitness over iterations to check convergence
plot(parent_obj$GA)

$selected_founders is a data frame with the indices (row numbers in the effect matrix) and individuals (names, as in the genotype file) of the selected parents. $GA is the ga object returned by the GA package. Useful parts include:

  • parent_obj$GA@fitnessValue — the ultimate GEBV of the best solution
  • parent_obj$GA@summary — the max, mean, q3, median, q1, and min fitness of the population at each iteration
  • parent_obj$GA@solution — every solution with the best fitness
  • parent_obj$GA@iter — the number of iterations run

The output contains the selected parent IDs and names. More information is available in the internal GA object about GA performance, change in the best localGEBV and meanGEBV of the parental sets over iterations, etc. There may be more than one set of parents that give rise to the same optimum. Additional sets of parents are contained in the GA object and only the first set is presented in $selected_founders

docs.title: Visualisations
docs.text:
HapSelect provides a collection of publication-quality ggplot2 visualisation functions for exploring marker effects, haplotype architecture, haploblock structure, and linkage disequilibrium.

All plotting functions return standard ggplot2 objects, allowing further customization using normal ggplot2 syntax.

#Examle of creating and modifying a HapSelect ggplot object

p <- marker_effects_plot(...)

p +
  labs(title = "Marker Effects") +
  theme_minimal()

As a special case:

We use default position values because of the ability to choose between genetic map position (cM) and physical map position (bp), the following is an example convert the positions on some graphs to Mb:

haploblock_plot <- haploblock_plot + scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(start, end, by), labels = as.character(seq(start, end, by) / 1e6), limits = c(start, end)) + labs(x = "Position (Mb)")

where breaks = seq(start, end, by / 1e6) controls where labels should go and seq is a function in R that takes a start position (where the x axis starts), an end position (where the x axis ends), and a by argument (where should labels be put on the x axis). The labels = as.character(seq(start, end, by) / 1e6) controls the names of the labels set by breaks and you will notice the entire sequence vector is divided by 1e6, or 1 million. This converts the labels into Mb. Similarly, 100 Kb increments can be defined by replacing 1e6 with 1e5 and Gb can be defined by replacing 1e6 with 1e9.

docs.title: Marker Effects Plot
docs.text:
Creates a Manhattan-style scatter plot displaying estimated marker effects across the genome.

marker_effects_plot(
  marker_effects = marker_effects$Effect, #these MUST be in the same order as the map file!
  chr            = map$Chromosome,
  pos            = map$Position
)

docs.title: Required Inputs
docs.text: Parameter Description marker_effects Numeric vector containing estimated marker effects chr Numeric chromosome identifier for every marker pos Genomic position corresponding to every marker

docs.title: Optional Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Description colors c("#A01FF0","#A7A8AA") Two alternating chromosome colors

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
• Missing values are automatically removed.
  • Marker effects, chromosome vector, and position vector must all have identical lengths.
  • Chromosomes are ordered numerically.
  • Returns a ggplot object.

Tip

If you have non-numeric chromosomes you must convert them into numerics. You can then re-map the numbered chromosomes into their non-numeric values using ggplot syntax. AI tools are incredibly helpful to help with this - either provide the source code or mention it is a Manhattan-plot style ggplot and you are trying to replace the chromosome labels with another set of labels.

docs.title: Haplotype Effect Visualisations
docs.text: These functions visualize estimated effects assigned to individual haplotypes or localGEBV in a Manhattan-style plot.

docs.title: Unique Haplotype Effects
docs.text:
Plots the estimated effect for every unique haplotype.

unique_haplo_effects_plot(
    haplo_obj = haploblock_obj
)

docs.title: Unique localGEBV Effects
docs.text:
Plots estimated local genomic breeding values for every unique haplotype.

unique_localGEBV_effects_plot(
    haplo_obj = haploblock_obj
)

docs.title: Block Variance Manhattan Plot
docs.text:
Displays estimated haploblock variance along the genome in a Manhattan-style plot.

block_variance_manhattan_plot(
    haplo_obj = haploblock_obj

docs.title: Required Inputs
docs.text: Parameter Description haplo_obj Object returned by compute_local_GEBV() or compute_haplotype_effects()

docs.title: Shared Optional Parameters
docs.text:
These apply to unique_haplo_effects_plot(), unique_localGEBV_effects_plot(), and block_variance_manhattan_plot().

Parameter Default Description colors c("#A01FF0","#A7A8AA") Alternating chromosome colours pos_type "midpoint" Position used to represent each haploblock

docs.title: Position Options
docs.text: Value Description "midpoint" Uses the midpoint of each haploblock "start" Uses the first marker position

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: A ggplot2 object.

docs.title: Haploblock Variance Visualisations
docs.text:
These plots examine the relationship between haplotype effects and estimated haploblock variance.

Internally, block variance is transformed using

log10(Block_Var)

before being min-max scaled to improve visualization.

docs.title: Haploblock Variance Funnel Plot
docs.text:
Plots haplotype effects against scaled haploblock variance.

haplo_block_var_funnel_plot(
    haplo_obj = haploblock_obj
)

docs.title: localGEBV Variance Funnel Plot
docs.text:
Plots localGEBV values against scaled haploblock variance.

local_gebv_block_var_funnel_plot(
    haplo_obj = haploblock_obj
)

docs.title: Generic Block Variance Funnel Plot
docs.text:
Maintained for backwards compatibility.

block_var_funnel_plot(
    haplo_obj = haploblock_obj
)

docs.title: Required Inputs
docs.text: Parameter Description haplo_obj Output from compute_local_GEBV() or compute_haplotype_effects()

docs.title: Optional Parameters
docs.text:
These apply to all three funnel plots.

Parameter Default Description mean_line TRUE Draw dashed mean variance line, change to FALSE to remove scale_colors c("blue","purple","red") Gradient colors for effect size on the x axis

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Larger values indicate higher estimated block variance.
  • Color represents effect magnitude.

docs.title: Haploblock Structure Plot
docs.text:
Displays haploblock boundaries across chromosomes.

plot_haploblocks(
    haploblock_df = haploblock_obj$Haploblocks
)

docs.title: Required Inputs
docs.text: Parameter Description haploblock_df Haploblock dataframe

docs.title: Optional Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Description block_fill "#A01FF0" Haploblock fill colour chrom_fill NA Chromosome background colour height 0.30 Chromosome track thickness single_width_bp NULL Width used to display single-marker blocks - mostly deprecated

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Transparent chromosome backgrounds are produced with chrom_fill = NA.
  • Single-marker blocks are automatically given a visible width if single_width_bp = NULL.

docs.title: Haploblock Variance Plot
docs.text:
Displays haploblock boundaries across chromosomes, like plot_haploblocks(), with each block coloured by its variance. This shows where the high-variance regions sit on each chromosome as well as how large the blocks are.

plot_haploblocks_variance(
    haploblock_obj = haploblock_obj
)

docs.title: Required Inputs
docs.text: Parameter Description haploblock_obj Object returned by compute_local_GEBV() or compute_haplotype_effects()

docs.title: Optional Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Description variance "Block_Var" Column of haploblock_obj$Haploblocks to colour blocks by, usually "Block_Var" or "Unique_Haplo_Block_Var" (see LocalGEBV) scale_viridis_option "magma" Viridis colour palette: "magma", "inferno", "plasma", "viridis", "cividis", "rocket", "mako", or "turbo" (or the equivalent letters "A" to "H") chrom_fill NA Chromosome background colour height 0.30 Chromosome track thickness single_width_bp NULL Width used to display single-marker blocks

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Variance is shown on its original scale (not log transformed), so a few very high-variance blocks will stand out against the rest. This can be manually scaled in the haploblock_obj$Haploblocks data frame
  • Single-marker blocks are automatically given a visible width if single_width_bp = NULL.
  • haploblock_obj must contain localGEBV/haplotype effects - a haploblock data frame from block_obj_to_df() alone does not have a variance column.

docs.title: Marker Density Plot
docs.text:
Plots marker density along chromosomes using fixed genomic bins.

plot_marker_density(
    map = map
)

docs.title: Required Inputs
docs.text: Parameter Description map Ordered marker map containing Chromosome and Position

docs.title: Optional Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Description bin_size 500000 Bin width used for counting markers (500 Kb default) height 0.30 Chromosome thickness chrom_fill NA Chromosome fill colour col_low "white" Low-density colour col_mid "purple" Mid-density colour col_high "red" High-density colour

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Smaller bins increase resolution.
  • Larger bins produce smoother density estimates.
  • Final bins are automatically truncated at chromosome ends.

docs.title: LD Decay Plot
docs.text:
Plots pairwise linkage disequilibrium (R²) as a function of physical distance.

plot_ld_decay(
    map = map,
    ld = ld_pairs
)

docs.title: Required Inputs
docs.text: Parameter Description map Marker map containing SNP names, chromosomes, and positions ld Pairwise LD dataframe

docs.title: Optional Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Description max_kb 500 Maximum pairwise distance method "gam_cr" Curve fitting method k 50 Number of basis functions for GAM span 0.30 LOESS smoothing span point_color "#A7A8AA" Scatter colour curve_color "#A01FF0" Fitted curve colour alpha 0.20 Point transparency

docs.title: Curve Options
docs.text: Method Description "gam_tp" Thin-plate regression spline GAM "gam_cr" Cubic regression spline GAM "exp" Exponential decay model "loess" LOESS smoother

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• "exp" produces a monotonic decay curve.
  • span only affects LOESS.
  • k only affects GAM fitting.
